items.title: El Rayo secures Tesco listing across 525 stores
items.summary: El Rayo secured a nationwide listing for its Plata tequila in 525 Tesco stores, expanding its presence across the UK grocery market. The deal adds Tesco to the independent spirits…
items.body:
El Rayo secures Tesco listing across 525 stores
El Rayo secured a nationwide listing for its Plata tequila in 525 Tesco stores, expanding its presence across the UK grocery market.
The deal adds Tesco to the independent spirits brand’s supermarket stockists, which already include Sainsbury’s and Waitrose.
The 100 per cent agave tequila is listed on Tesco’s website at £35 for a 70cl bottle, with an ABV of 40 per cent.
El Rayo founder and chief executive Tom Bishop said: “Tesco is a major milestone for us.”
He said the listing would help the brand reach more shoppers as it seeks to broaden tequila’s appeal beyond shots into longer drinks and cocktails.
Tesco spirits buyer Antonia Karkides said the retailer was seeing growing interest in tequila across different occasions and serves, alongside demand for brands offering something different.
Founded in 2019, El Rayo has built its proposition around serves such as tequila and tonic. Its range also includes ready-to-drink Tequila Tonic & Grapefruit and Tequila Lime & Soda.
Alongside its retail distribution, the brand is served in more than 1000 hospitality venues nationwide, including Sushi Samba, Forza Wine and Cubitt House.

items.title: The Entertainer owner’s losses widen despite record £315m sales
items.summary: The Entertainer owner Teal Group posted record annual sales of £315 million, but pre-tax losses widened to £19 million as costs mounted. Sales rose 10 per cent from £286.6 million in the year to January 31, 2026. Pre-tax losses increased from £10.1 million, while operating losses doubled to £16.8 million. Adjusted EBITDA stood at £2.9...
items.body:
The Entertainer owner Teal Group posted record annual sales of £315 million, but pre-tax losses widened to £19 million as costs mounted.
Sales rose 10 per cent from £286.6 million in the year to January 31, 2026. Pre-tax losses increased from £10.1 million, while operating losses doubled to £16.8 million. Adjusted EBITDA stood at £2.9 million.
The group blamed higher employment costs, business rates, depreciation and exceptional charges, including its move to employee ownership.
It also incurred £5.4 million in one-off costs establishing its largest retail partnership.
Trading strengthened after the year end, with like-for-like sales at The Entertainer’s own stores rising 22 per cent in the first half and sales across all channels increasing 13 per cent.
The improvement followed the Grant family’s transfer of ownership to an employee ownership trust in September 2025, enabling Sunday opening and broader product ranges.
Teal also invested £5 million in lower prices and restructured to remove £10 million from operating costs from 2027/28.
The board expected profitability to improve significantly this year. Several store openings are planned for 2027, including at least three in the UK’s top 20 retail locations.

items.title: Retail spending stalls as shoppers hold out for Black Friday deals
items.summary: UK retail sales rose 1.5 per cent in October, but shoppers held back on big-ticket purchases ahead of Black Friday and Christmas. The latest BRC-KPMG figures, covering the four weeks to October 31, showed growth was slightly below the 1.6 per cent recorded a year earlier but above the three-month average of 1.2 per cent....
items.body:
UK retail sales rose 1.5 per cent in October, but shoppers held back on big-ticket purchases ahead of Black Friday and Christmas.
The latest BRC-KPMG figures, covering the four weeks to October 31, showed growth was slightly below the 1.6 per cent recorded a year earlier but above the three-month average of 1.2 per cent.
Food sales increased 3.2 per cent, while non-food sales were flat as customers delayed purchases of furniture and white goods.
In-store non-food sales fell 1.1 per cent, compared with growth of 0.1 per cent last October. Online non-food sales rose 1.8 per cent, taking online penetration to 38.6 per cent from 38.2 per cent a year earlier.
British Retail Consortium chief executive Helen Dickinson said: “October was subdued for retailers, as shoppers delayed spending ahead of Black Friday and Christmas. Big ticket categories, such as furniture and white goods, performed badly as customers waited for November deals.”
Dickinson said wet weather helped online sales, while Halloween falling on a Saturday boosted spending on snacks, costumes and decorations.
She added: “Retailers are hoping pent-up demand translates into stronger spending through November and December, as they work hard to deliver great choice and value for households this Christmas.”
KPMG UK head of consumer, retail and leisure Linda Ellett said clothing, footwear and duvets benefited from falling temperatures, but higher household costs and uncertainty ahead of the Budget limited overall growth.
“Nonetheless, growth will be welcomed by a retail sector that desperately needs to offset cost increases with some strong sales as the promotional and festive season gets into full swing,” she said.
IGD chief executive Sarah Bradbury said half term and Halloween supported grocery spending, potentially alongside households stocking up following the government’s Be Ready campaign.
However, she warned shoppers remained pessimistic about their finances.
“Food and grocery promotions should help keep shoppers spending during the festive period, but we expect January to be a difficult month for many households,” Bradbury said.

items.title: Cadbury connects with THG Ingenuity for new direct-to-consumer gifting platform
items.summary: Cadbury has appointed THG Ingenuity to power its new direct-to-consumer Cadbury Shop.This will see THG Commerce deliver a cloud native digital storefront and interactive customisation software, THG Studios produce end-to-end e-commerce creative assets and visual digital merchandising,
items.body:
Cadbury has appointed THG Ingenuity to power its new direct-to-consumer Cadbury Shop.
This will see THG Commerce deliver a cloud native digital storefront and interactive customisation software, THG Studios produce end-to-end e-commerce creative assets and visual digital merchandising, while THG Fulfil will provide warehousing, pick-and-pack, temperature controlled confectionery handling, courier management and customer service solutions.
Central to the launch is an interactive product customisation engine developed to power the flagship Cadbury Heroes Pick & Mix, which allows shoppers to hand-pick a combination of miniature favourites.
The platform also introduces on-demand personalisation across giftboxes, including the dedicated Cadbury Build Your Own Letterbox Gift service, where shoppers can pick any six Cadbury tablets to be packaged and delivered straight to someone's doorstep.
Darren Rajanah, Chief Revenue Officer, THG Ingenuity, says: “We are proud to power the next phase of Cadbury’s commerce journey. Delivering exceptional direct-to-consumer experiences requires more than just a storefront; it demands an integrated operating environment where engaging creative content and intelligent digital technology connect seamlessly with automated fulfilment."
"By uniting THG Commerce’s e-commerce capabilities with THG Studios’ creative production and THG Fulfil’s operational scale, we are equipping Cadbury with the infrastructure needed to scale their direct-to-consumer personalised gifting business with confidence.”
Philip Warfield, Marketing Director, Cadbury - Mondelēz International, says: “Cadbury has always been about generosity and bringing people closer together. Appointing THG Ingenuity and launching the new Cadbury Shop gives us an exciting way to do exactly that ahead of Christmas, combining the chocolate the nation loves with beautifully personal gifting experiences, from the moment you choose it to the moment it's opened."
"It's a unified end-to-end solution that pairs personalisation, visual storytelling and fulfilment, helping us turn every gift into something truly special and serve our customers better than ever before.”
2026 RTIH Innovation Awards
E-commerce was a key focus area at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards.
The awards celebrate global retail technology innovation in a fast moving omnichannel world. Our winners were revealed at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC in Central London on Wednesday, 4th November.
The event consisted of a drinks reception, three course meal, awards ceremony presided over by award winning stand-up comedian, presenter, actor and broadcaster, Aurie Styla, and after party until 1am.

items.title: Waitrose reunites Keira Knightley and Joe Wilkinson for Christmas ad sequel
items.summary: Waitrose has reunited Keira Knightley and Joe Wilkinson for its 2026 Christmas campaign, launching a six-minute sequel to last year’s festive romantic comedy. ‘The Perfect Gift 2’, which premiered on YouTube and Waitrose.com on November 10, also stars Alex Hassell as Hugo Bunty-Griffin, a new love rival for Wilkinson’s character Phil. Waitrose said the film...
items.body:
Waitrose has reunited Keira Knightley and Joe Wilkinson for its 2026 Christmas campaign, launching a six-minute sequel to last year’s festive romantic comedy. ‘The Perfect Gift 2’, which premiered on YouTube and Waitrose.com on November 10, also stars Alex Hassell as Hugo Bunty-Griffin, a new love rival for Wilkinson’s character Phil. Waitrose said the film was the longest advert produced by a UK supermarket, running two minutes longer than last year’s instalment. Created with Wonderhood Studios and directed by Molly Manners through Biscuit Filmworks, the sequel follows Phil’s attempt to win back Knightley with a homemade beef Wellington. Waitrose’s festive range features throughout, including its No.1 Handmade Polar Bear Bao Buns, to build on its ‘Home of food lovers’ positioning.
Waitrose chief customer officer Nathan Ansell said: “Last year demonstrated that emotional, entertainment-first storytelling effectively cuts through the festive noise, builds strong brand affinity, and creates genuine cultural momentum.” He added: “With this ambitious sequel, our goal is to build on that connection, bring our story full circle, and give audiences a compelling reason to return.” MG OMD led the media strategy, planning and buying for the wider campaign, which takes inspiration from a film release with trailers, cinema advertising and romcom-style posters. Activity will run across TV, video on demand, cinema, print, outdoor, audio, social and online channels, alongside PR and in-store marketing. The full film will sit on Waitrose’s owned channels, supported by 60-second and 30-second trailers. Separate product adverts will feature the cast alongside items from the Christmas range, including No.1 Ham & Cheese Croissant Stacks and No.1 Pistachio & Sour Cherry Frangipane Mince Pies. The launch will also be supported by a press junket, behind-the-scenes footage, bloopers, cooking content with @whatwillycook and a partnership with Meet Cutes London. items.title: What are Britons buying on Whatnot? Auction site reveals top items from darts trading cards to old M&S clothes
items.summary: Online selling platform Whatnot has exploded in popularity this year, as Britons bid on everything from trading cards to the latest toys and sold-out trainers.
items.body:
What are Britons buying on Whatnot? Auction site reveals top items from darts trading cards to old M&S clothes
The online selling platform Whatnot has exploded in popularity this year, as Britons bid on everything from trading cards to the latest toys and sold-out trainers.
Whatnot's most popular feature is its live auctions, where sellers can flog their wares on video in real-time and buyers swipe to make bids.
The website has become known as the place to go if you are looking to buy into the latest internet craze or viral sensation.
In 2026 it has been a hub for people selling Labubus, Pokémon cards and vintage clothing from the early 2000s.
But what will be the hot items for sellers in 2027? Whatnot has trawled through its search and purchase data to reveal what buyers want right now, and what will be popular next year.
Hot item: Small stress toys called Squishies were one of the biggest selling products on the auction website Whatnot this year, with searches rising 100-fold
Toys
Toys are big business, as the number of adult collectors looking to relive their childhoods grows.
The next wave of nostalgia centres on the 1990s and 2000s, according to Whatnot.
In particular, it predicts a boom for Shrek Lego collections as fans combine their love of nostalgic toys with revived interest in the popular 2001 film.
Orders for Shrek Lego figures recently spiked 30-fold in a month after a new edition was released.
Jellycats, the popular cuddly toys with smiley faces, are still very popular, with orders up 13-fold in 2026.
Rare characters like the Luxe Bunny fetch 77 per cent more than a typical Jellycat. This year, the highest-selling Jellycat went for £850.
And it's vital to keep them in mint condition if you want to make a big profit.
Daniel Fisher, head of categories & expansion, Europe at Whatnot, said: 'Condition, completeness and rarity make the biggest difference when reselling.
'On Whatnot, a Jellycat with its tags still on sells for 37 per cent more than one without.'
Squishies, the squeezable polyurethane toys in the shape of animals or food items, have replaced Labubus as Britain's breakout toy according to Whatnot.
Searches for squishies went up 100-fold this year while Labubu searches fell 89 per cent.
PS3 consoles and games are also set to boom as the console turns 20 in March 2027. Searches increased by 360 per cent on Whatnot in 2026.
Trading cards
Pokémon's popularity has risen seismically over the years, with some trading cards originally worth just a few pence now selling for close to £2,000.
Originally named Pocket Monsters, Pokémon started out as a game released for the Nintendo Gameboy in Japan in 1996.
It's 30th anniversary in September brought in hundreds of thousands of first-time buyers to Whatnot. Many were original fans who grew up in the late 1990s and early 2000s.
Searches for Vintage Pokémon cards went up 164 per cent last year, while the Charizards and Eevees were the most-searched Pokémon.
Whatnot said buyers are building collections around favourite characters and the cards that mean something to them.
In the UK, football is still the backbone of card collecting. Arsenal cards have led the way in 2026 with orders up 490 per cent after the club's Premier League-winning season.
But Liverpool cards are Whatnot's hot tip for 2027. The club has inched ahead since the new season kicked off with Florian Wirtz and Virgil van Dijk among the most-bought players.
And with the Women's World Cup arriving in 2027, women's football is set to have its collecting moment too.
The number of sellers going live with darts cards has also more than tripled, with orders up more than 30-fold in 2026.
This could be a sweet spot for sellers, as darts auctions on Whatnot sell 2.6 times as many cards as typical sports card shows.
Vintage Pokémon card searches are up 164% as collectors look for their favourite characters
Arsenal card orders are up 490% after the club's Premier League-winning season
Fashion
Whatnot shoppers are looking for quality over quantity, the platform says, as British shoppers gravitate towards timeless fashion items over fleeting trends.
Searches for Mulberry, the quintessentially British luxury fashion and leather goods brand known for its iconic handbag styles like the Bayswater and Alexa, jumped by 500 per cent this year.
Buyers can still find bargains, though. In October, a Vintage Mulberry Daria Hobo bag sold for £285. On Mulberry's official resale site, they can sell for around £500.
Coach, another popular handbag brand, saw its searches rise by 600 per cent.
Marks & Spencer resale clothing is also popular with searches up 26 per cent.
Whatnot's Fisher said: 'Check your loft for childhood favourites and well-kept vintage pieces from the likes of M&S, Coach or Mulberry, and hold on to any tags, boxes and dust bags, as they all help increase item's value.'
Classic accessories are also being restyled in new ways. Searches for floral brooches have increased by 202 per cent, big sunglasses by 68 per cent, and silk scarves by 78 per cent.
On the whole, fashion generates more orders than any other category on the platform, with order volume more than doubling since last year.
The number of fashion buyers and sellers has also doubled year on year. This could be down to two reasons.
One, a lack of graduate jobs prompting a surge in side hustles. And two, a generation of 'doom spenders' splurging on luxuries instead of saving for a property or other milestones they feel they might never afford.
Now could be a great time to start selling clothes on the side as the tax-free trading allowance is set to treble from April 2027.
Mulberry: Bags from the iconic brand are selling well on Whatnot, as a cheaper alternative to new pieces such as this Vintage Oak Suede Bayswater bag which costs £1,245 brand new
Beauty
Korean beauty will continue to be a staple of skincare routines in 2027, Whatnot predicts.
In 2024, the Korean beauty market was worth about £9.75billion. By 2030, this could be £14.3billion according to forecasts.
K-beauty brands accounted for more than 80 per cent of skincare orders on Whatnot's platform, and Korean and Japanese brands' share of UK beauty orders rose 860 per cent over the last year.
Medicube, a popular Korean brand appears to be taking centre stage, with UK searches up 60-fold in 2026.
Whatnot says fragrance is a big trend for 2027, and this is being driven by British men with searches for men's aftershave soaring 400 per cent.
Dior Sauvage, Parfums de Marly Layton and Creed Aventus are among the fragrances proving particularly popular.
The number of men buying beauty in Whatnot's auctions grew by 630 per cent this year meaning there are roughly around 7.3 times as many male beauty buyers compared to last year.
On top of this, the amount of money men spent on beauty grew by 800 per cent, making the total spend roughly 9x higher.
Medicube is a popular Korean derma-cosmetic brand booming on TikTok

Morrisons has gone live in its first store with Emerald, the UK grocery retailer's new checkout software. It is working with NCR Voyix on the project.
In a LinkedIn post, Laura Critchley, Support Office Specialist- Front End Operations, said: "This is a project that I, alongside so many fantastic colleagues across the business, have been working on for the last two years, so seeing it finally come to life in store is a brilliant feeling."
She added: "Emerald will replace our existing Storeline software across checkouts and cash offices, bringing a more streamlined, modern and user-friendly experience for colleagues, while helping to make everyday processes easier and improve the customer experience."
"It’s been a huge collaborative effort to get us to this point, and it’s fantastic to see all the hard work starting to pay off. A brilliant step forward for our Front End teams, and we can’t wait to see Emerald rolled out across our stores from next year."
2026 RTIH Innovation Awards
Morrisons was named Overall Winner at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, which took place in Central London last week. And it also emerged victorious in the RTIH Editor's Choice category for its partnership with Gatekeeper Systems.
In a LinkedIn post, the retailer said: "We’re delighted to have been named Overall Winner, selected by the judging panel as the standout entry from across all of the event's 23 categories. Great recognition for some of the brilliant and innovative cross functional projects that have been delivered over the last few months!"
It added: "We were also recognised in the Editor’s Choice Award, alongside Gatekeeper Systems for our Cart Control programme across five Morrisons stores. The programme has delivered some fantastic results: An estimated 82.1 tonnes of CO₂e saved each year; 1,170 fewer replacement trolleys needed; 7,696 fewer trolleys ending up in local communities and waterways. Congratulations to everyone involved in making this possible!"
Scott Thompson, Editor and Founder at RTIH, said: "Congratulations to Morrisons. We received a record number of entries this year, showcasing truly impressive innovation across both traditional and digital retail spaces."
"To quote a member of our judging panel: Reviewing such inventive, high impact solutions has been a truly rewarding experience. The depth of engineering, scalable architecture, and strategic vision displayed throughout the submissions underscores the rapid transformation happening across modern retail technology."
"A number of companies were in the running for Overall Winner but ultimately the judges picked Morrisons for launching several innovative initiatives encompassing major technological upgrades to enhance its customers’ shopping experience."

items.title: US retailer DeCicco & Sons expands Simbe Store Intelligence technology roll-out following pilot
items.summary: US grocery retailer DeCicco & Sons has expanded Simbe’s Store Intelligence platform chainwide following a 35% reduction in out-of-stocks within the first 60 days at its pilot locations. Simbe’s autonomous shelf scanning robot, Tally, captures detailed shelf conditions multiple times daily. That
items.body:
US grocery retailer DeCicco & Sons has expanded Simbe’s Store Intelligence platform chainwide following a 35% reduction in out-of-stocks within the first 60 days at its pilot locations.
Simbe’s autonomous shelf scanning robot, Tally, captures detailed shelf conditions multiple times daily. That intelligence flows into the retailer’s existing systems, helping teams identify and resolve issues faster while supporting applications spanning store operations, e-commerce, and business intelligence.
“Our customers count on us to have the products they love and a team ready to help,” says John DeCicco Jr., CEO, DeCicco & Sons. “Simbe helps us deliver on both. Digitising our shelves is foundational to our broader technology strategy, because it gives every system we run an accurate picture of what’s happening in our stores. With real-time visibility into stores, our teams can address corrective fixes sooner and spend more time providing the personal service that brings people back to DeCiccos.”
A critical element of DeCicco & Sons’ success has been integrating physical intelligence directly into existing workflows. Rather than requiring store teams to adopt another standalone tool, Simbe connects shelf-level data to the systems and routines they already use. This approach enables associates to stop searching for issues and focus on resolving them instead, while giving business teams access to a consistent, accurate understanding of store conditions.
“Having better information about our shelves helps us take better care of our customers and our team,” says Chris Dapolito, Manager at DeCicco & Sons, Sleepy Hollow. “I’m spending more of my day out in the store, talking with shoppers and supporting our department managers. Those relationships are a big part of what makes DeCiccos special, and Tally helps us build on them.”
“DeCicco & Sons recognised early that the future of retail operations depends on continuous understanding of what’s happening inside physical stores,” says Caitlin Allen, SVP, Market at Simbe. “By connecting that intelligence to the systems and people running its business, DeCiccos is demonstrating how physical AI can elevate shopper experience, empower associates, and lay the foundation for increasingly autonomous retail.”
2026 RTIH Innovation Awards
Automation was a key focus area at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards.
The awards celebrate global retail technology innovation in a fast moving omnichannel world. Our winners were revealed at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC in Central London on Wednesday, 4th November.
The event consisted of a drinks reception, three course meal, awards ceremony presided over by award winning stand-up comedian, presenter, actor and broadcaster, Aurie Styla, and after party until 1am.

items.title: How to get the buzz back on Britain’s high streets | Letters
items.summary: Readers respond to an article about the decline of town centres Sammy Gecsoyler’s report from Rotherham ( ‘It’s just vape shops, nail shops, charity shops’: can anything save the British high street?, 4 November ) tells the story in its dates. One out-of-town retail park in Britain in 1981; 385 by 1996. Parkgate opened in 1987 and MPs warned that it would disembowel towns and villages. It did. Rotherham town centre is now 24% vacant, while retail park vacancy nationally sits at 4.8%. That is not a mystery. It is 40 years of planning policy. We have since gone one step further by making home delivery cheaper than retail parks. Up to 3bn parcels a year now land on British doorsteps and not one of them passes through a town centre. Continue reading...
items.body:
Sammy Gecsoyler’s report from Rotherham (‘It’s just vape shops, nail shops, charity shops’: can anything save the British high street?, 4 November) tells the story in its dates. One out-of-town retail park in Britain in 1981; 385 by 1996. Parkgate opened in 1987 and MPs warned that it would disembowel towns and villages. It did. Rotherham town centre is now 24% vacant, while retail park vacancy nationally sits at 4.8%. That is not a mystery. It is 40 years of planning policy.
We have since gone one step further by making home delivery cheaper than retail parks. Up to 3bn parcels a year now land on British doorsteps and not one of them passes through a town centre.
Andy Burnham’s £210m for high streets is welcome, but is a one-off against a structural problem. What a town centre needs is a reason for people to walk into it again, every week, without being told to.
So here is a proposal, given in written evidence to an inquiry by the Commons housing, communities and local government committee into revitalising high streets. Put £1 on every parcel delivered to a residential address. Charge nothing if it is collected from a shop, locker or pickup point in town. Ringfence the money by law and return it to the council area that the parcel landed in – 60% to transport and 40% to markets and high streets.
The pound is not the point; the exemption is. The cheapest way to receive a parcel would involve walking into a town centre. That would do more for Rotherham than any grant.
 
Dan Johnson
 
Co-founder, Crafty Vintage, Whalley, Lancashire
I run the Grumpy Cook, a community-focused cafe in Hastings. I’ve seen first-hand how difficult it is for independent businesses to survive, particularly in communities where disposable income is already stretched. That’s why I recently launched My Local First, a loyalty and rewards platform to bring independent businesses together. Customers earn rewards for spending locally, discover other independent businesses and have a reason to return. Businesses can participate for just £10 a month, without paying commission on their sales to the platform.
But high streets cannot thrive if the people living around them cannot afford to participate in their local economy. That’s why we’re also developing ways to connect affordable food and discreet community support.
We cannot expect councils or government grants alone to regenerate town centres. Nor can we expect individual businesses to compete with multinational corporations on their own. We need to start working collectively. My Local First won’t solve every problem facing Britain’s high streets. But it represents something I believe we’ve lost sight of: communities taking responsibility for their own local economies. Perhaps the answer isn’t simply saving our high streets. Perhaps it’s giving people a reason to believe in them again.
 
Barry Ashley
 
Hastings, East Sussex
As someone who grew up locally, I recognise the challenges in Rotherham. The new government strategy, Hope on the High Street, has some ideas – including a number of community-led schemes that we helped support at the Architectural Heritage Fund. Projects like High Street West in Sunderland – a mixed-use approach to derelict shops that delivered a cafe, music venue and workspaces. Or Valley Heritage’s development in Bacup, Lancashire, where a Grade II former bank has been split into co-working space and affordable housing.
Equally importantly, it’s about empowering these communities as they are passionate about their environment. Although there are many challenging town centres, a growing number offer a more positive future and could be replicated elsewhere.
 
Matthew Mckeague
 
CEO, Architectural Heritage Fund
Saving the British high street means accepting that retail can no longer be its primary purpose. Councils should acquire vacant or persistently underused sites and, where appropriate, replace poor-quality empty buildings with well-insulated, low-rise homes for renters and young professionals. New developments could be designed from the outset so that extra floors or modular homes can be added later as demand grows. That would cost more initially, but could reduce the disruption and expense of future expansion.
Housing alone, however, will not make a thriving neighbourhood. It should be interspersed with services and spaces that people genuinely need: walk-in health and mental health support, childcare, community and arts spaces, and other local amenities. There is a strong case for locating services closer to the communities they serve, rather than expecting people to travel elsewhere to find support. High streets should also include more and better green spaces, with trees, planting and small parks that give people somewhere pleasant to spend time, while at the same time responding to the challenge of climate change and air pollution.
Bring people back to the high street and businesses will have a reason to return too: cafes, hairdressers, independent shops and other everyday services. Councils should use planning and licensing powers carefully to encourage a balanced mix of businesses and avoid excessive concentrations of premises that can undermine the health and character of an area. The high street will not be saved by restoring the past. Its future could lie in becoming a place to live, meet, access services and build community, with retail as one part of a much broader purpose.
 
Helen Roberts
 
Sheffield

items.title: Poundland unable to buy new stock as fears over collapse grow
items.summary: The discount chain is continuing to edge towards collapse and is said to be "running on fumes", according to one insider.
items.body:
Poundland unable to buy new stock as fears over collapse grow
- Published
Poundland is unable to buy new stock to fill its shelves after being blocked by its owners from accessing cash in its bank accounts.
The discount chain is on the brink of collapse with one insider describing it as "running on fumes". It has until Thursday to secure a rescue deal.
About Â£50m has been frozen by its American owner Gordon Brothers, the BBC understands, meaning its 600 shops are running out of stock.
Pressure is building on Gordon Brothers, which bought Poundland for Â£1 last June, after the owner rejected a takeover bid that could have saved the thousands of jobs currently at risk. Gordon Brothers has been approached for comment.
Poundland has filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators, which protects it from its creditors until Thursday.
Access to funds was limited because of a tension between Gordon Brothers' dual role as both creditor and shareholder, a source said, but added they expected a relaxation of funds in the next two days.
Last week, Poundland boss Barry Williams told staff like-for-like sales, which exclude new store openings, were up 11.4% last week, which included Halloween, but said this was Â£1.5m ahead of budget.
He said the business made a profit of Â£18.1m in the year to September, which was a "strong recovery" from the previous year where the business made losses of Â£68m.
The latest annual accounts have yet to be audited.
- Burnham 'ready to support' Poundland staff as retailer faces collapse 
  - Published29 October
- Poundland staff protest after chain approach administrators 
  - Published29 October
However, Gordon Brothers has painted a different picture of the business, saying the chain remains "challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading".
It said it had provided significant funding to support the company's ability to trade since it acquired the business.
It has also made Â£18m, from a combination of debt interest payments and other fees and charges.
On Wednesday, executives from Gordon Brothers will appear before the Business Select Committee with MPs probing whether they are genuinely pursuing a solvent rescue of the business, which has 11,000 employees, and whether every realistic step is being taken to protect jobs and stores.
The session is being held in private given commercially sensitive discussions are still under way with bidders.
Uncertain future
On Thursday, the 10-day moratorium to protect Poundland from its creditors expires, but if there is a prospect of a solvent deal, the deadline could be extended.
If not, Poundland is set to collapse into administration and could be broken up.
A source familiar with the sales process said London-based Xyra Group was making "significant progress" in its last minute bid to buy Poundland and could now be the front runner.
An extension of Thursday's deadline now seems an increasingly likely scenario. But such a case would be difficult to put forward if Gordon Brothers continues to block funding.
One observer remarked "if Gordon Brothers is going in front of that committee, you don't want to be giving the message we're pulling up the drawbridge".
Even if a deal is agreed to sell the business as a whole, there is no guarantee a new owner would not reduce the number of stores, but suppliers to Poundland would prefer that outcome to hundreds of sites being sold off to other retailers.
There has been interest from the likes of Poundstretcher, Tesco and B&M in picking up stores which could mean continuing employment for many workers.
The central issue is whether a piecemeal sale would protect more jobs than a buyer willing to keep Poundland trading as a national chain.

items.title: The hottest product in Britain this year? A 2kg bag of ice
items.summary: As the UK endured record-breaking temperatures this summer, nothing grew in popularity on Deliveroo like sacks of sweet relief from the supermarket Iceland Name: Iceland’s 2kg bag of ice. Age: The first patents for commercial mechanical production date to the 1850s. Continue reading...
items.body:
Name: Iceland’s 2kg bag of ice.
Age: The first patents for commercial mechanical production date to the 1850s.
Appearance: Clear, cold.
Just normal ice, then. Ice in its most desirable form.
Cubes, you mean. A bag containing 2kg of ice cubes, as sold by the British supermarket Iceland.
What’s so desirable about that? “These ice cubes are better than anyone else’s and are great value for money,” according to a five-star review on Iceland’s website from Trevor P.
So Trevor likes ice. Not just Trevor. According to Deliveroo, Iceland’s 2kg ice bag was the “top trending” UK delivery order – a metric that marries year-on-year growth in orders, relative order volume in the local area and customer ratings – of 2026 so far.
Really? What came second? The diavola pizza from Monte Forte Neapolitan Pizza in Horsham, West Sussex.
How specific. But ice bag deliveries from Iceland were so popular in London that they came second in Deliveroo’s global ranking.
I guess it was a pretty hot summer. The hottest since records began.
How much would a 2kg bag of ice set me back on a scorching July afternoon? You can get one for £1 in the store.
That’s not bad, actually. But when you add in the Deliveroo surcharge, its small-order fee, the delivery fee, the bag charge and the service charge, it could cost as much as £8.
That’s ridiculous! As I’ve pointed out, you could get the same bag from the shop for a quid.
Yeah, but the shops are, like, hundreds of metres away. You could even make your own ice, in your own freezer, for a fraction of the cost.
But then I’d have to realise I’ll want a margarita hours before I do. I prefer to be spontaneous. Do you not see the irony of paying over the odds to have someone bring you a single bag of ice amid a climate crisis?
The climate crisis is why I want the ice. A climate crisis brought about in no small part by the rapacious demands of western consumerism, all because you can’t be bothered to fill your own ice trays?
OK, I do see the irony, but my hands are tied. No they aren’t! You can make better choices!
Anyway, it’s November now. I’m cold and I want soup. Well, the good news is you can probably make a lovely soup from things you already have in your kitchen.
I don’t like that kind of soup. What kind of soup do you like?
Soup from a man in a motorbike helmet. I despair.
Do say: “When we’re having ice delivered while the world burns, something is seriously wrong with our priorities.”
Don’t say: “This pizza from Horsham – can I get it delivered to Peterborough?”

items.title: Shopping or social? What an under-16 ban could mean for resale
items.summary: As ministers consider bringing online marketplaces into the proposed social media ban, eBay, Vinted and Depop face a question that cuts to the heart of social commerce: where does shopping end and social networking begin? Follow a seller, scroll through a personalised feed, message about a jacket and make an offer. On peer-to-peer marketplaces, shopping...
items.body:
As ministers consider bringing online marketplaces into the proposed social media ban, eBay, Vinted and Depop face a question that cuts to the heart of social commerce: where does shopping end and social networking begin?
Follow a seller, scroll through a personalised feed, message about a jacket and make an offer. On peer-to-peer marketplaces, shopping and social interaction are often part of the same journey.
That overlap could become a regulatory headache for the resale sector as the UK government considers whether its proposed ban on social media for under-16s should extend to online marketplaces.
For eBay, Vinted and Depop, the stakes go beyond losing access to younger shoppers. Restrictions could affect how buyers discover products, how sellers build a following and how the two sides communicate before a sale.
Yet their inclusion is not confirmed. The central question is whether ministers will regulate platforms according to their primary purpose — buying and selling — or the risks created by the social features built around transactions.
Why marketplaces are in the frame
The prospect moved beyond a theoretical debate on 8 November, when Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said the government was seriously considering extending the proposed ban to online marketplaces.
Speaking on the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Nandy said ministers were examining the move as part of efforts to protect children from online harm.
The concern is not simply what children can buy. It is who can contact them while they browse and trade.
The Children’s Society has warned that some young people are being approached through resale platforms and asked for indecent photographs in exchange for money or gifts.
These services also have a young audience. Ofcom research found that 19 per cent of children aged eight to 14 use eBay at least monthly, while 15 per cent use Vinted.
That puts marketplaces at the intersection of two competing considerations: protecting children from harmful contact and preserving access to services whose main function is commerce rather than social networking.
When a shop becomes a social network
On paper, the distinction looks straightforward. eBay, Vinted and Depop connect people who want to buy and sell goods. But profiles, private messages, following, recommendations and personalised feeds make the experience more social than a conventional online checkout.
Depop illustrates the blurred boundary particularly clearly. Its social-commerce model lets users follow sellers, discover products through feeds and interact with other members. The community and the shop are closely connected.
This creates a difficult choice for policymakers. Treat every marketplace with social functions as a social network and the restrictions could reach well beyond their original target. Focus only on a platform’s commercial purpose and the risks associated with private contact could remain.
More than a loss of young shoppers
If marketplaces fall within a blanket ban, the most immediate consequence would be the exclusion of under-16 users. For resale businesses, however, those users can sit on both sides of the transaction.
A younger participant may be buying affordable second-hand clothing one day and selling unwanted items the next. Removing that access could therefore affect both demand and the supply of goods, rather than simply reducing a platform’s audience.
The implications would vary. Depop’s fashion-led community makes its appeal to younger consumers particularly relevant. Vinted could face disruption to younger users’ clothing resale activity, while eBay’s exposure would span a broader range of product categories.
The wider question for second-hand retail is whether restrictions would narrow young people’s opportunities to earn money from unwanted possessions and take part in circular shopping. The size of any commercial impact would depend on the final rules and the users they cover.
Keeping under-16s off affected services would also raise a practical challenge: establishing who is old enough to use them.
More robust age verification could introduce additional compliance costs and extra steps at registration. Marketplaces face a potential tension between demonstrating effective safeguards and keeping the buying and selling journey straightforward.
Ofcom has identified photo ID matching, digital ID, banking checks and facial age estimation as methods capable of providing highly effective age assurance at 16. Which approach affected marketplaces might adopt, and how it would fit into their services, remains an open question.
Could messaging be the dividing line?
An alternative to excluding younger users entirely would be to target the features that expose them to harmful contact.
That could mean tighter restrictions on communication between strangers. But messaging is not merely a social extra on a resale platform: it allows buyers to ask about an item’s condition, negotiate a price or arrange a collection.
Restricting those exchanges could leave younger users able to browse while limiting their ability to complete the interactions that support a purchase. The challenge would be to separate necessary trading conversations from unsafe contact without undermining the marketplace itself.
A defining test for social commerce
The government has said the first regulations for its proposed under-16 social media ban will be laid before Parliament by the end of 2026, with initial restrictions expected in spring 2027. Whether eBay, Vinted and Depop will be included remains unresolved.
A platform-wide age restriction could affect customer acquisition, transactions and stock coming onto services. Feature-specific safeguards could leave younger users able to participate, but change how they discover sellers and communicate with them.
The debate exposes a tension at the centre of social commerce. Features that make online shopping feel personal and community-driven can also create channels for harmful contact.
The question is no longer simply whether they are shops or social networks. It is whether the rules can address the risks of being both without removing the interactions that help them function.

items.title: AI joins the Christmas ecommerce rush — but will recommendations turn into sales?
items.summary: With UK festive online spending forecast to hit £28.52bn, retailers face a new contest for visibility, trust and conversion as shoppers turn to AI for gift inspiration and better deals. The battle for Christmas spending may begin before a shopper reaches a search engine, let alone a website. A request for a gift within a...
items.body:
With UK festive online spending forecast to hit £28.52bn, retailers face a new contest for visibility, trust and conversion as shoppers turn to AI for gift inspiration and better deals.
The battle for Christmas spending may begin before a shopper reaches a search engine, let alone a website. A request for a gift within a particular budget can now produce an AI-generated shortlist, this leaves brands with a new challenge – making sure they are on it.
The opportunity comes against a backdrop of forecast growth. Research from Adobe predicts UK shoppers will spend a record £28.52bn online between 1 November and 31 December, up 6.2 per cent year-on-year. Fourth-quarter ecommerce sales are expected to climb 6.4 per cent to £40bn.
AI is expected to play a bigger role in how that spending is directed. Adobe forecasts that traffic to retail websites from AI platforms will rise 214 per cent year-on-year during November and December, compared with a 111 per cent increase in September.
That does not mean AI is responsible for the overall increase in sales, or that shoppers are ready to hand over their wallets to autonomous assistants. The research and industry commentary point to a more nuanced shift. AI is helping consumers decide what to buy, while retailers work out how to be recommended, and how to turn that recommendation into a completed order.
A new route to the Christmas shortlist
PayPal research finds that 35 per cent of UK consumers are already using, or planning to use, AI to help with their Christmas shopping. Finding deals or comparing prices is cited by 52 per cent, while 51 per cent point to product research. Personalised gift recommendations and identifying this year’s must-have presents each attract 39 per cent.
Dave Jones, head of UK consumer at PayPal, describes shoppers as “embracing new ways to make their lives easier”, including “using AI to compare deals and take some of the stress out of Christmas and gift buying”.
These more detailed requests could reveal needs that a conventional search leaves unclear. Simon James, managing director of AI & data strategy at Publicis Sapient, says: “The average Google search is four or five words. The average AI prompt is around twenty. That gives retailers a much richer picture of intent, because you start to understand the ask behind the ask.”
He points to B&Q’s assistant as an example of helping customers work out what they need for a project, rather than simply directing them to an individual product. The potential commercial benefit is a fuller basket, although that remains an opportunity rather than a guaranteed outcome.
Winning a recommendation, not just a click
The shift creates a different kind of competition for visibility. Tom Bowie, co-founder at Ignite Stack, says its research with Visible PR analysed 600 AI-generated answers to Christmas gifting questions. John Lewis appeared in around one in five responses, while Monica Vinader, LEGO and Hampers.com led their respective gifting categories.
“It’s no longer just about competing on price, advertising or search rankings,” Bowie notes. “Brands also need to make sure they’re appearing in the AI recommendations that increasingly influence what shoppers consider buying.”
Those findings describe visibility within the answers studied, not a share of Christmas sales. But they illustrate why retailers are paying attention to the point at which consumers assemble their shortlist.
Cathy Farmer, head of GEO at Third City, argues that retailers need to answer specific needs rather than rely on broad promotional language.
“Someone asking for a gift for a particular person, budget and interest needs a useful recommendation, not a page of generic claims,” she says. “I’d focus on clear product information, up-to-date availability and credible independent coverage that helps explain who a product is right for.”
This does not make other marketing channels irrelevant. Adobe also forecasts that revenue share from social networks will rise 24 per cent, with influencer partnerships up seven per cent. Jack Rigby, founder of PR Barn, argues that media coverage, social referrals, reviews and an easy-to-search website all contribute to AI visibility.
Farmer cautions: “A place in an AI answer is worth checking, but it isn’t a sale. Retailers need to look at what happens next: visits, purchases and whether those customers come back.”
The sales impact may be harder to track
Measuring those outcomes presents another challenge. Daisy Wolfenden, managing director at Wolfenden, reports strong growth in revenue coming directly from AI platforms across its retail clients, while stressing that it remains a small proportion of overall sales.
“AI is influencing which retailers consumers discover, which products they consider and ultimately where they spend, but much of that influence won’t be reflected in direct referral revenue,” she says. “A customer might discover a brand through ChatGPT and then purchase through Google or directly with the retailer.”
That distinction matters when assessing AI’s contribution this Christmas. Referral traffic can show one route to a purchase, but Wolfenden’s point is that discovery and checkout may happen in different channels. Looking only at sales attributed directly to an AI platform could miss some of its influence.
Conversational tools may also help explain why shoppers do not buy. James says an assistant can capture where a conversation stopped and which questions went unanswered, exposing barriers such as delivery charges.
“Web analytics only ever showed clicks,” he says. “This starts to show you people’s motivations and barriers.”
Discovery is ahead of delegation
Growing use of AI for inspiration should not be confused with a willingness to let it spend. Research from Signicat highlights how trust changes with the task: 42 per cent of consumers would trust AI to create recipes and 38 per cent to draft emails, but only eight per cent would be happy for it to make high-value purchases on their behalf. For smaller purchases, the figure is 19 per cent.
The research also finds discomfort with AI making purchases on a consumer’s behalf at 69 per cent, close to the 71 per cent recorded for opening financial products. That points to a boundary between seeking advice and allowing a tool to make financial decisions.
Mark Howell, director of EMEA retailers at Rithum, puts the distinction plainly: “The biggest impact of AI right now isn’t autonomous purchasing, its discovery. People are increasingly using AI tools as search engines.”
This switch therefore makes a stronger case for improving discovery and decision-making than for assuming shoppers will delegate the entire transaction.
The promise has to survive checkout
Even a well-targeted recommendation can fall short if the retailer cannot fulfil it. Product data, availability and the checkout experience connect AI-led discovery to actual revenue.
Joe Squire, marketing director at Epos Now, describes a shopper asking an assistant to find a gift under £40 that can be collected that day. In that scenario, he argues, accurate, connected stock information becomes crucial.
“That makes a retailer’s stock data its new shop window,” he notes. “An independent shop with a website and a till that don’t talk to each other risks being invisible at exactly the moment a shopper is ready to buy.”
The next hurdle is completing the order. Nikhita Hyett, EMEA general manager at Signifyd, says: “If AI helps someone find the right product at the right price, only for their order to be declined at checkout, the entire experience falls apart.”
Her warning is that fraud checks must distinguish genuine purchases from risky ones as shopping journeys change. Behind the transaction, staffing also matters: Kristján Freyr Kristjánsson, co-founder and CEO of 50skills, argues that automating contracts and onboarding can help retailers get seasonal workers ready sooner, allowing fulfilment to keep pace with customer expectations.
AI’s impact on UK ecommerce this Christmas is therefore unlikely to be captured by one traffic-growth figure. The forecasts suggest a fast-growing route into retail websites; the consumer research shows demand for help with prices, products and presents, alongside continuing reluctance to surrender control of purchases.
The opportunity is not simply to appear in more AI answers. It is to be recommended for the right reasons, offer the product the shopper actually needs and make the purchase work. A place on the Christmas shortlist is valuable — but the sale still has to be earned.

items.title: Poundland ‘frontrunner’ Xyra Group asks retailer’s founder to join bid
items.summary: The little-known investment firm emerging as a “frontrunner” to buy Poundland has called on Steve Smith, the retailer’s founder, to bolster its bid for the struggling firm.  Xyra Group Holdings, founded by 23-year-old Manvedeep Singh, has asked Smith to lend support to their £12.5m bid to keep Poundland afloat as the discount retailer veers towards [...]
items.body:
Poundland ‘frontrunner’ Xyra Group asks retailer’s founder to join bid
The little-known investment firm emerging as a “frontrunner” to buy Poundland has called on Steve Smith, the retailer’s founder, to bolster its bid for the struggling firm.
Xyra Group Holdings, founded by 23-year-old Manvedeep Singh, has asked Smith to lend support to their £12.5m bid to keep Poundland afloat as the discount retailer veers towards collapse, City AM has learned.
Smith has had conversations with Xyra Group in recent days but does not plan to take part in any takeover efforts until a deal has been completed, it is understood.
The Poundland founder, who set up the retailer with his father, Kevin Smith, in 1990, had been weighing investing in the company himself or backing a rival offer tabled by Martin Property Group but has ruled out both options.
Gordon Brothers, the US investment firm which owns Poundland, is racing to find a solvent buyer for the retailer before a moratorium blocking creditors from calling in their debt lapses on Thursday.
The firm’s filing of a notice to appoint administrators had sparked fears Poundland was edging towards collapse but it is now holding talks with multiple bidders over a sale of the company as a going concern.
Gordon Brothers’ earlier attempts to find a solvent buyer for Poundland had been derailed over its demand to be paid £22.5m for a loan it inherited from PepCo, the retailer’s previous owner, when it bought the firm for £1 last year.
PepCo owns £7.5m of this loan, which is worth £30m in total, but has offered to defer its repayment.
Jobs at risk from collapse
Xyra Group is offering to pay Gordon Brothers £12.5m up front, leaving a £10m shortfall on the investment firm’s share of this loan. Martin Property Group has offered to pay £5m initially, leaving a shortfall of £17.5m, it is understood.
This makes Xyra Group the “frontrunner” to acquire Poundland, sources told City AM. While there had been questions over the source of the investment firm’s funding, it has made “significant progress” in providing proof of “credible backing,” they said.
Xyra Group has not completed a single acquisition since it was founded in November 2024 and little is known about its senior leadership. Viktor Bronzovic, who serves as its chief executive, is a 27-year-old tech entrepreneur and former DJ.
Gordon Brothers has faced significant political pressure in recent weeks, prompted by fears that the retailer’s collapse would put its 12,000 staff and 600 stores at risk.
On Wednesday, the US investment firm will appear in front of parliament’s business select committee, where it will be grilled on its efforts to find a credible buyer for Poundland.
Xyra Group was contacted for comment. Gordon Brothers declined to comment.

items.title: Why retail colleague safety must remain a priority all year round | Viewpoint: Beth Worrall
items.summary: Nobody should have to worry about their safety when they arrive at work, but for too many retail colleagues, the prospect of violence and abuse has become very real. Now, the National Week of Action to Protect Retail Workers is shining a very important spotlight… This story continues at Why retail colleague safety must remain a priority all year round | Viewpoint: Beth Worrall Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
Figures from the BRC at the beginning of the year revealed that as many as 1,600 incidents happen daily. While this is an improvement on the previous year, the scale of the problem remains deeply concerning.
VoCoVo research reveals the impact this is having on teams and retailers, with almost nine in ten (88%) seeing colleagues leave their roles because of physical or verbal abuse from a customer. It’s a significant human impact – people going to work are fearing intimidation and can experience wellbeing issues long after an incident has happened.
Retailers are very much aware of the issue and are taking action to help solve it, with collaboration across the sector playing a valuable role in driving progress. The National Week of Action provides an important opportunity to recognise this, bringing the industry together to share experiences, learn from one another and continue listening to colleagues about where they feel most vulnerable.
The industry state of play
Retail colleagues are often on the receiving end of wider frustrations and pressures in society, despite having little control over the issues that customers may be angry about. But there have been some genuine steps forward to turn the tide. The Crime and Policing Bill covers a standalone offence for assaulting a retail worker, which sends a very clear message that retail teams shouldn’t be expected to deal with the current situation.
There are also some very encouraging developments in the role of collaborative technology. London-based retailers have integrated new reporting tools to submit CCTV footage within minutes to police forces. This led to an increase from 7.3% to 29.4% in reported shoplifting cases resulting in a caution.
The ability for retailers to share information with emergency services and other stakeholders is valuable in tackling organised groups and repeat offenders. Shared intelligence can give teams the power to identify patterns and respond effectively to persistent offenders. For smaller retailers, such as convenience stores with fewer resources, this data can be especially valuable.
In other cases, retailers should be sharing intelligence with each other so they can refine their strategies for future incidents. Collaboration also matters just as much within the stores themselves. When communication is easy, colleagues have the tools and confidence to reach out whenever they need support.
Helping colleagues feel supported
Clear lines of communication among teams are crucial to dealing with an unfolding incident. Whether it’s another colleague, store manager or an external security team, colleagues need a way of discreetly alerting others when they feel threatened. Communication tools, such as headsets, can help facilitate this, giving teams instant access to support. This is vital for colleagues working in isolation, such as in convenience stores late at night, giving them reassurance that help is readily available.
A combination of technologies can provide an additional layer of protection, helping colleagues feel safer. Measures such as CCTV and real-time alerts allow colleagues to keep a close eye on suspicious activity and react quickly, while AI-powered tools are analysing live footage and automatically identifying potentially suspicious behaviour. Depending on the potential danger posed by the situation, colleagues can either take steps to prevent it from escalating or alert emergency services.
Pairing this technology with clear incident response procedures and structured training can ensure a more coordinated, connected approach and instil greater confidence in teams at the same time.
Momentum needs to be sustained
The National Week of Action to Protect Retail Workers is an important opportunity to build momentum, but meaningful progress will depend on the retail industry maintaining its focus on colleague safety throughout the year. Stronger legislation is a great starting point, but more intelligence sharing and advances in technology all have a role to play in helping to protect people on the shop floor.
The success of these efforts should be measured by how safe and supported colleagues feel when they come to work. By taking a more connected and proactive approach, retailers can give their teams the confidence that help is always available and that they will never be expected to face abuse alone.
Beth Worrall, is CEO of VoCoVo

items.body:
Tackling operational refund delays with instant gift card options
When a customer shops online and needs to return an item, for example to exchange it for a different size, refunds to a bank card can typically take 3-5 working days to process. This delay can interrupt what is often a non-linear shopping journey, where customers want to re-purchase quickly.
To give customers more control, New Look introduced an optional refund to giftcard. Customers can actively choose this at the point of return with 12 months to spend the balance, or continue with a traditional refund to their original payment method.
For those who select the gift card option, funds are issued digitally as soon as the returned item reaches the distribution centre, allowing customers to re-shop sooner and manage their money more easily.
Beyond the immediate use case, the solution plays a strategic role in customer retention by keeping value within the New Look ecosystem. Rather than driving a single transaction, it encourages repeat engagement and supports an ongoing relationship between the customer and the brand.
Challenge
New Look identified an opportunity to improve the customer experience at a key moment in the shopping journey: returns and refunds. While online shopping volumes continued to grow, traditional refund processes were not always aligned with customer expectations for speed, flexibility, and digital-first experiences.
In particular, customers returning items in order to exchange for a different size or style were often required to wait several days for a refund to be processed to their original payment method before placing a new order. At the same time, New Look wanted to move away from paper-based credit notes and create a more consistent experience across in-store and online channels.
Alongside these customer experience goals, the business looked at how its existing gift card program could play a bigger role, making gift cards a core part of the business rather than a brand awareness tool.
Solution
Working with Edenred Payment Solutions, alongside existing partners ZigZag and Voucher Express, New Look launched a new refund to gift card proposition.
The solution is offered as an optional alternative during the returns process, allowing customers to actively select a gift card refund if they want faster access to their money, or to continue with a standard refund to their original payment method.
For customers who choose the gift card option, an eGift card is issued digitally as soon as the returned item arrives at New Look’s distribution centre.
Funds are available to spend immediately online or in-store, either on a replacement item or a future purchase.
Edenred Payment Solutions provides the underlying payments capabilities powering the programme, including closed-loop gift card issuance, processing, balance enquiries, top-ups, and redemption, across virtual gift cards.
The result is a more flexible, digitally enabled refund experience for customers, while supporting New Look’s wider goals around retention and brand engagement as a natural by-product of improved customer choice.
“Edenred Payment Solutions are more than a supplier. They are a partner that allows us to continually innovate and improve the customer experience. Their gift card expertise gives us the confidence to test new ideas and deliver more flexible journeys for our customers,” said Jessica Hartnett, B2C partnerships mMarketing manager, New Look.
Results
Since launching in October 2024:
- Over £2M retained within the business
- 4% uplift in customers choosing the refund to gift card option
- £270k retained within the business in one month, as refunds were re-spent rather than paid out
- 42% of customers redeemed their gift card on a subsequent purchase
- 48% uplift in basket value when customers redeemed a gift card compared to standard purchases
Conclusion
New Look’s refund to gift card programme demonstrates how optional, digitally enabled refunds can better support modern shopping behaviour, where returns and re-purchases often happen close together.
By giving customers faster access to their money and greater choice at the point of return, New Look has improved flexibility at a key moment in the customer journey.
At the same time, the programme has helped strengthen loyalty and repeat purchase, showing how customer-first design can also deliver meaningful commercial outcomes when supported by the right payments infrastructure.

items.title: Comet brand returns as an electricals marketplace
items.summary: Discover what's happening in retail today, Retail Times publishes international & UK retail news covering products, data, tech, packaging, people, research, comment and much more. Fourteen years after disappearing from Britain’s high streets, one of the country’s most recognisable electricals brands has officially returned, complete with its famous black and orange identity and a new ambition to become the UK’s go-to destination for tech and electricals. First founded in 1933, Comet was part of British life for generations, the place […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Fourteen years after disappearing from Britain’s high streets, one of the country’s most recognisable electricals brands has officially returned, complete with its famous black and orange identity and a new ambition to become the UK’s go-to destination for tech and electricals.
First founded in 1933, Comet was part of British life for generations, the place millions of families went for a new television, washing machine, games console or their latest bit of tech.
Now, more than 90 years after the name first appeared, Comet has been rebuilt for the way Britain shops today.
The new Comet launches online with more than one million products spanning TVs, mobile phones, computing, gaming, cameras, kitchen appliances and household electricals.
While the familiar name and colours are back, the old retail model isn’t. Rather than holding its own stock, Comet has returned as a dedicated electricals marketplace, bringing products from 2,500 sellers together in one specialist destination.
Cas Paton, CEO of Comet, said: “Ask almost anyone in Britain about Comet and they’ll have a memory attached to it. It might be the first TV they bought when they moved out, the family computer, a games console at Christmas or the washing machine they suddenly couldn’t live without.
“Comet is a brand that still has such a positive impression on so many people. That connection hasn’t gone away, and now we have the opportunity to bring it back for a whole new generation.
“But this isn’t about trying to recreate the Comet of the past. We want to take that nostalgia, history and trust and build something for the way people shop today. Our ambition is simple: when you need something that plugs in, we want Comet to be the first place you think of.”
The relaunch is backed by a £10 million investment as Comet looks to re-establish itself as a major force in UK electricals.
For Paton, the ambition is to ultimately build Comet into a £1 billion business. With the backing of a famous British brand and a marketplace model built for modern shoppers, the focus is on reaching that milestone as quickly as possible.
Comet’s return also creates a significant new sales opportunity for businesses operating across the electricals market.
Unlike a traditional retailer, Comet does not compete with sellers by offering its own inventory. Instead, every sale made through Comet is a sale for one of the retailers or brands on the marketplace, giving them a new route to UK shoppers under one of the most recognised names in British electricals.
Paton added: “Every sale that’s made on Comet is a sale for another retailer. We’re a friend of the retailers. We’re here to attract customers, build trust and give customers choice.”
“We want to bring some competition back to the market, but in a way that creates opportunity for retailers and brands too. Comet already means something to British shoppers. Our job now is to turn that recognition into customers and sales for the businesses selling through us.”
Comet is now welcoming new sellers ahead of its first peak trading period, as it continues to expand the range available through the marketplace.
Retailers and brands interested in selling through Comet can find more information here.

The Spar store, located between Brampton and Haltwhistle on the major A69 trunk road, has undergone a complete refurbishment and an expansion of floorspace. Around 400sq ft has been added to […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Spar North of England retailer M&L Richardson & Sons Ltd are reaping the benefits from a refit at their Low Row store and forecourt.
The Spar store, located between Brampton and Haltwhistle on the major A69 trunk road, has undergone a complete refurbishment and an expansion of floorspace.
Around 400sq ft has been added to its size to accommodate a new kitchen area which has been incorporated as part of the development work, taking the space to 1,500sq ft in total.
Driving this change is the introduction of an enhanced Food To Go offering which includes a hot Clayton Park Bakery food unit. Two new Cheeky Coffee machines have also been installed too, both dispensing iced coffees, to support demand for on-the-go customers.
The comprehensive changes have also seen new energy efficient refrigeration installed throughout, modern space saving shelving has been installed, bright LED lighting fitted, and a new customer counter introduced.
Externally, the Shell forecourt is enjoying a spruce up with the latest graphics and branding, and new lighting has been fitted around the canopy.
Low Row is where things began for the Richardson family business in 1968. Nestled on the picturesque border of Cumbria and Northumberland, and a stone’s throw from Hadrian’s Wall, it became part of Spar in 2003 when the Richardsons partnered with James Hall & Co. Ltd.
Martyn Richardson is one of four brothers who are directors of M&L Richardson & Sons Ltd alongside David, Kevin, and Paul. His niece, and David’s daughter Ellie, is the first of the next generation of Richardson family members to join the business.
Martynsaid: “We are very pleased with the look and feel of the Low Row store and a huge thank you to our team and to the various departments at James Hall for their work in bringing the transformation to life.
“The development has been positive and sales have improved. We made the changes really to take greater advantage of Food To Go, especially putting in the Cheeky Coffee brand and the Clayton Park Bakery unit has meant we can improve margin and introduce link deals.”
The Richardsons have continued to grow and invest in their business over the years, currently sitting at 11 sites across Cumbria, Northumberland, and County Durham.
A standalone Spar store on English Street in central Carlisle was opened in October 2024 within the same month that the family acquired a forecourt site at Edens Lawn in Haltwhistle.
Planning has also been approved to redevelop the family’s forecourt and Spar store at Crossways in Gretna, and Spar Frizington in West Cumbria has been given the green light by planning too for an expanded, much-improved community store and brand-new forecourt.
Martyn added: “We must keep progressing. Now we have Ellie working with us as the next generation of the family, learning the business, delivering the same level of service our customers expect, and bringing in new ideas to help drive it forward.”
Ellie said: “We are known as the garage with the nice view on the A69, and when you hear that from customers who regularly stop here, I think that is quite heartwarming.
“I started in the business as I wanted to be working after the pandemic where I lost a little motivation for academic study. I switched to do a Level 2 Retail Apprenticeship instead and I immediately loved it.
“It is a crazy, demanding and fast paced industry with plenty of variety – you see new faces and deal with regular customers daily. I can say for definite that no day is the same. I have washed cars, covered shifts on the tills, and I have helped manage the car workshop at Low Row.
“I am training up to be an Area Manager, but my focus currently is the Spar store at Low Row, particularly after the recent store refit and expansion to include the kitchen. Food hygiene and safety is vital with food service and that is a growing part of the business.”
James Hall & Co. Ltd is a fifth-generation family business which serves a network of independent SPAR retailers and company-owned Spar stores across Northern England six days a week from its base at Bowland View in Preston.

The new Holborn Megastore, located at 1 Thavies Inn, Holborn Circus, offers more than 10,000 sq ft of retail space and over […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch!
