items.title: Co-op Group and Southern Co-op merger gets CMA approval
items.summary: Co-op Group and Southern Co-op have today (5 November) received approval from the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) to join forces, marking a significant milestone for both organisations. The approval follows the Transfer of Engagements earlier this year, which saw Southern Co-op's businesses transfer to… This story continues at Co-op Group and Southern Co-op merger gets CMA approval Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
The approval follows the Transfer of Engagements earlier this year, which saw Southern Co-op’s businesses transfer to a wholly owned subsidiary of Co-op Group.
The businesses can now begin the process of coming together, combining more than 300 years of co-operative heritage.
The move brings together Southern Co-op’s 173 food stores, 69 funeral homes and around 330,000 members with Co-op Group’s 2,300 food stores, 800 funeral homes and 7.5 million members.
As part of the remedies agreed to secure CMA approval, 15 convenience stores and two funeral homes across the combined estate will be divested.
Both businesses will continue to operate as normal while migration plans are finalised, with no immediate changes to membership benefits or rewards.
Kate Allum, interim chief executive, The Co-operative Group, said: “Today is a significant moment for our two societies and the wider co-operative movement. CMA approval gives us the green light to begin an exciting new chapter of co-operation.
“By bringing together more than 300 years of co-operative heritage, we have the opportunity to build an even stronger Co-op, with greater scale and resilience, and the ability to deliver more for our members, customers and communities.”
Ben Stimson, chief executive, Southern Co-op, said: “We can now build on Southern Co-op’s achievements and take the strengths of our business forward into the next chapter. I’d like to thank colleagues and members for their continued support.
“Our priority is to maintain our shared values and strengthen the co-operative movement as we join forces in earnest. We’ll keep supporting our colleagues and serving our customers and clients brilliantly through the transition.”

Shoppers, streetscapes and 188 years of Australian style: David Jones through the years – in pictures
A fixture of city centres and a launchpad for local fashion designers, Australia’s oldest department store is facing an uncertain future after entering into voluntary administration this week
Carmen Dell'Orefice, a prominent model, is captured in 1950 during David Jones’ American fashion parade in Sydney. The photograph, taken by Geoffrey Lee, highlights the fashion trends of the era and Dell'Orifice's role in popularising US fashion in Australia. Photograph: Alamy
Thu 5 Nov 2026 09.00 ESTLast modified on Thu 5 Nov 2026 23.29 EST
The David Jones store in Sydney’s Elizabeth Street in 1931. The store, opened in 1927, remains the company’s flagship location to this day.Photograph: State Archives Collection, Museums of History NSW
Workers in David Jones’s Surry Hills garment factory in 1946. About half of the women working in manufacturing in Sydney in the 1940s worked in the ‘rag trade’.Photograph: State Archives Collection, Museums of History NSW
The David Jones coronation choir performing in the Elizabeth Street store in Sydney during June 1953. The event marked the celebrations of Queen Elizabeth II’s coronation.Photograph: Alamy
What was then the largest Union Jack flag in the world, 100ft by 50ft (30 by 15 metres) and made in England, hanging from David Jones’s Sydney store for the Queen’s 1954 royal tour.Photograph: JR T Richardson/Fox Photos/Getty Images
The entrance to the Monaro Mall, which housed a David Jones store, in Canberra in 1966. The mall was later named the Canberra Centre.Photograph: National Archives of Australia
Sydney’s George Street store, 1969. The original site of Welsh merchant David Jones’s drapery business, the George Street store continued to trade until it was sold in the early 1970s.Photograph: City of Sydney
The Elizabeth Street store, 1989. From 1944 to 1985 the store housed an art gallery that hosted artists including Sidney Nolan, Arthur Boyd and Russell Drysdale.Photograph: City of Sydney
The David Jones store in central Canberra, 1987. The retailer now has 38 stores in Australia and one in New Zealand.Photograph: D Thomas/National Archives of Australia
Australian swimming star Ian Thorpe launches his men’s underwear range IT, sold exclusively in David Jones, in 2003.Photograph: Patrick Riviere/Getty Images
Designers pose together after the fashion parade for David Jones’s summer 2005 collection launch at the W Hotel in Sydney.Photograph: Patrick Riviere/Getty Images
Australian model and David Jones ambassador Megan Gale (sixth from left) parades an outfit by Australian designer Akira during the David Jones winter in 2006. Photograph: William West/AFP/Getty Images
International model Heidi Klum appears in a live window display for the launch of her new line Heidi Klum Intimates at the Elizabeth Street store in 2015.Photograph: Caroline McCredie/Getty Images
David Jones’s flagship store in Bourke Street in Melbourne. The retailer’s head office was moved from Sydney to Melbourne in 2016. Photograph: Speed Media/Alamy

items.title: Deals on meals | In focus: Meal for tonight
items.summary: The weekly shop may still have its place, but for many consumers the question of what to eat that evening is increasingly answered much closer to dinnertime. That creates an obvious opportunity for convenience stores, whether shoppers want a ready meal they can heat in… This story continues at Deals on meals | In focus: Meal for tonight Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
That creates an obvious opportunity for convenience stores, whether shoppers want a ready meal they can heat in minutes, the ingredients for something freshly cooked or the makings of a more indulgent ‘big night in’.
Aagrah Foods, the Indian cooking sauces specialist, describes meal for tonight as the fastest-growing shopping trip, accounting for one in five grocery visits, with shoppers increasingly opting for smaller baskets and convenient meal solutions rather than eating out.
John O’Neill, retail operations controller at wholesaler Parfetts, takes a similar view. “It is a massive growth opportunity as time-poor shoppers increasingly rely on convenience stores for evening solutions,” he says. “Retailers can capitalise by turning their stores into hassle-free destinations, ensuring their range is visible and easy to navigate.”
Changing routines
Hybrid working is also changing when the mission takes place. The traditional stop-off on the evening commute is no longer the only time shoppers think about dinner.
Booker says more people spending part of the week at home means meal decisions are increasingly made during local shopping trips, lunchtime visits or through on-demand delivery, rather than always at the end of the working day. Ian Taylor, retail and brand development director at Spar UK, says this is spreading the occasion more evenly across the week.
“Rather than one big Friday night treat occasion, we’re seeing meal for tonight spread much more evenly across midweek, as people working from home part of the week are around to shop locally in the afternoon and want something easy for that evening,” he says.
This means the mission encompasses rather more than emergency ready meals. Parfetts recommends a mix covering shoppers who want maximum convenience and those happy to do some cooking, including ready meals, chilled pizzas and pies alongside fresh produce, pasta and sauces.
O’Neill also points to the need for a mix of familiar brands and value alternatives. Booker takes a similarly broad view, dividing the opportunity between fresh ingredients and meal components, chilled ready meals, pizza and sharing products, pies and savouries, and frozen foods.
Fake-away favourites
One of the clearest trends is the desire to recreate something closer to an eating-out experience at home, but minus the price-tag. “Shoppers want restaurant-style experiences at home without the premium price-tag, driving demand for high-quality chilled meals and quick-cook ingredients,” says O’Neill.
“Restaurant-style pizza deals and quick pasta kits are performing particularly well.” Spar also identifies frozen as a growing part of the mission. Its partnership with Iceland Foods brings brands including Greggs, TGI Friday’s, Harry Ramsden and Slimming World into participating stores, giving shoppers another route to a quick ‘fake-away’ alongside fresh and chilled options.
Portion size is changing too. Spar has expanded its ready meal range with larger Classic Lasagne and Cottage Pie options intended for two, reflecting demand from couples as well as single shoppers and families.
Booker highlights several other trends, including global flavours, air fryer-friendly products, healthier choices and the continuing importance of value. At the same time, shoppers still want premium or restaurant-inspired options when the occasion calls for them.
Cooking solutions
Scratch cooking also has a role, provided it does not become too time-consuming. Shezad Aslam, managing director of Aagrah Foods, says shoppers are looking for “ready-to-use, premium quality and authentic ingredients” that make it easier to put together a meal quickly. “Shoppers are increasingly turning to scratch cooking to prepare meals that deliver restaurant-quality dishes and authentic flavours but which don’t require hours of preparation.”.
World foods therefore fit naturally into the occasion. Aslam says Indian food sits at the heart of the trend towards more-adventurous tastes, with shoppers increasingly seeking authentic flavours and products with clear provenance.
He also identifies personalisation as an important development, with shoppers choosing their own base, spice level and accompaniments rather than simply picking up a pre-set ready meal. That approach lends itself to linked purchases. A cooking paste may lead to naan, poppadoms, rice or a drink, just as pasta can be teamed with sauce, garlic bread and grated cheese.
Complete package
Indeed, the ability to sell a complete meal rather than a series of individual products is one of the strongest themes running through meal for tonight. Taylor at Spar says: “A dedicated section makes the occasion easy to shop and encourages shoppers to build a bigger, more complete basket.” He suggests bringing products such as wine, beer, pizza, snacks and treats together rather than forcing shoppers to visit several parts of the store.
Booker similarly identifies cross-category merchandising as one of the biggest opportunities, pointing to pizzas or burgers with beer, wine or soft drinks; pasta with sauces, garlic bread and cheese; and ‘fake-away’ displays bringing together mains, sides, sauces and drinks. For Parfetts, the same principle can extend to meal deals.
“Creating clear meal deals such as a main, side and a drink for a fixed price encourages extra spend while delivering the value consumers are looking for,” says O’Neill. Aagrah also points to meal deals and multi-buys as ways of giving shoppers a clear route to a complete dinner, while offering a spread of cuisines can broaden the appeal of the offer in-store.
Hot prospect
Meal for tonight does not necessarily have to come from the chiller or freezer. Hot food-to-go has traditionally been strongest at breakfast and lunchtime, but there is scope to stretch the offer further into the evening. O’Neill describes this as “a significant margin-boosting opportunity”, with fresh pizza, baked savouries and rotisserie lines among the options that can appeal to commuters looking for something they can eat almost immediately.
Booker also sees evening food-to-go as a way of capturing extra missions, particularly through pizzas, hot sandwiches, bakery products and meal deals, although it stresses the importance of matching the offer to local demand.
Clear signposts
Whatever form the offer takes, visibility is crucial. Spar recommends occasion-led merchandising backed by simple point-of-sale, while Parfetts favours clear signage and grouping products together near the front of the store, or in a dedicated chilled section. That sums up the meal for tonight mission neatly. Shoppers may arrive with a firm idea of what they want, or they may simply know they need dinner.
Either way, the opportunity for independents lies in having enough choice to provide an answer – and making that answer easy to spot.

items.title: Asos faces hit of up to £8m from cyber attack putting a dent in its turnaround efforts
items.summary: The retailer said the attack - which took place nearly a month ago and saw customers alerted to a breach through the Asos mobile app - had hit group sales by around 2 to 4 per cent in October.
items.body:
Asos faces hit of up to £8m from cyber attack putting a dent in its turnaround efforts
Fast fashion brand Asos has suggested sales were hit by up to £8 million after last month’s cyber hack - denting momentum behind a turnaround.
The online retailer said the attack - which took place nearly a month ago and saw customers alerted to a breach through the Asos mobile app - had hit group sales by around 2 to 4 per cent in October.
It suggests the attack has shaved between £4 million and £8 million off sales.
But bosses were eager to claim that the impact would be ‘temporary’ and that Asos is pushing ahead with a revival plan. Chief executive Jose Antonio Ramos said the impact had ‘dissipated’ in November.
The fashion retailer said authorities were still investigating after an ‘unauthorised party accessed some basic customer data.'
Last month, users of its app received a notification with a message titled 'ASOS HACKED', that read: 'Dear Asos DPO and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance. Engage with us, or we will leak it.'
Asos fell victim to a cyber attack just as it was hoping to win over the City with proof a revival plan is working
While customer names and contact details appear to have been stolen, Asos said no payment information or passwords had been compromised.
The retailer enjoyed booming business during the Covid lockdowns, but has struggled in the years since due to waning demand, rising costs and greater competition from the likes of ultra-cheap Chinese behemoth Shein.
It has tried to stem the decline by ridding itself of excess stock and clamping down on returns, even taking steps to ban customers from its platform.
Earlier this year, it sold its Lichfield warehouse to rival Marks & Spencer for £66million.
Retailer M&S fell victim to a hack last year that saw its shops left with empty shelves and its website down for six weeks. Harrods and Co-op were also attacked in a wave of cyber crime.
Fears around cyber security still loom large as European supermarkets, including in France and Belgium, have had their refrigerator systems hacked and the temperatures turned to high heats.
Ramos said that cybersecurity is ‘one of the areas where we are always putting a lot of focus and a lot of emphasis, and we have always been investing in it.’
He added: ‘So it's not that what happened last year was a wake up call for us or anything like that. We've always been investing.’
‘My concern is protecting our consumers and giving them confidence that Asos is the right place to buy.’
Attempting to brush aside worries around cybersecurity, the retailer pointed to signs of green shoots in its turnaround.
It swung back into the black for the year to 30 August, with £24.4million profits against losses of £281.6 million the previous year.
And it said sales returned to growth for the first time in four years over the final three months of this period.
And it said sales will grow by a low-single-digit range in the year to August 2027, compared to a 5 per cent fall in the previous year.
Ramos said ranges that were doing well at the moment include lace, satin, and sheer fabrics.
Mark Crouch, market analyst at trading platform Etoro, said: ‘Asos is beginning to look like a fashion retailer with a future again, rather than one permanently clearing up the mistakes of its past.
'Years of painful restructuring are finally producing results, with healthier margins, returning customers and the first quarterly sales growth since 2022 suggesting its long-awaited recovery is gaining substance.’

items.body:
Second buyer makes rescue bid for Poundland as retailer faces collapse
- Published
A second buyer has made a rescue bid for Poundland as the discount retailer teeters on the brink of collapse, with thousands of jobs at risk.
London-based Xyra Group has offered to pay off half of Poundland's outstanding debts - a key sticking point in takeover talks so far - immediately. The rest would be deferred.
With Poundland close to collapse, US-based owners Gordon Brothers have already rejected a rival bid from an Irish property group which would have saved its 12,000 staff.
Gordon Brothers said the business has faced years of instability and "remains challenged and vulnerable".
Sources familiar with the offer said Xyra is offering to immediately pay off Â£12.5m of an outstanding Â£30m loan on Poundland's books.
The offer came as Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds held crunch talks with Gordon Brothers about the future of the business, urging the investment firm to protect staff however possible.
Gordon Brothers, which bought Poundland for Â£1 last June, committed at the meeting to prioritise offers which protect its shops and workers.
The company said: "We are pursuing all avenues through the sale process to find a solution which protects as many jobs as possible and preserves value. Work continues at pace, engaging in active discussions on offers with interested parties."
Xyra is offering to pay off a higher proportion of Poundland's outstanding debts than Martin Property Group, which previously submitted a bid that Gordon Brothers rejected.
But doubts remain about the credibility of Xyra's offer, as there is little evidence they meet Gordon Brothers' tests, including whether they have the money and whether they would be good long-term owners of Poundland.
Sources pointed to the appointment of Andrew Brode to Xyra's board as a sign of its credibility. Brode works for RWS - a company that provides AI solutions for businesses.
Judith MacKenzie, head of Downing Fund Managers, told the BBC Brode is "well known and very credible" among small businesses in the UK.
But she said there is "hardly any information" publicly available about Xyra. "So, although some of the people look good, I can't find any evidence to say that they've got the money to back it up yet," MacKenzie added.
Gordon Brothers said: "Our intent throughout the comprehensive sale process has been to protect as many jobs as possible and preserve value in order to deliver the best available outcome for all the people, creditors and local communities who care about this business as much as we do."
Both Reynolds and Prime Minister Andy Burnham have questioned why a deal for the future of Poundland has not yet been made.
Though Xyra made an offer to take over the whole business, it is unclear whether it would keep Poundland together as its owner or break the company up.
Several Poundland suppliers have said they would also go bust if the retailer collapses. Its founder Steve Smith said two or three thousand suppliers to the firm, those who solely work for Poundland, would be caught up in the collapse.
He added that not only would Poundland's 12,000 staff be affected in that case, but potentially up to 30,000 overall.

items.title: ‘Shop owners are working people too’, retail body tells Treasury
items.summary: The British Independent Retailers Association (Bira) has called on the Treasury to explain why ministers do not regard employers as working people. Bira has hit back after chief secretary to the Treasury Emma Reynolds said at the weekend that employers are not working people. Speaking on… This story continues at ‘Shop owners are working people too’, retail body tells Treasury Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
Bira has hit back after chief secretary to the Treasury Emma Reynolds said at the weekend that employers are not working people.
Speaking on GB News on Sunday, Reynolds said: “I don’t think employers are working people, they are companies.”
The remarks have reignited the row over Labour’s 2024 manifesto pledge not to raise taxes on working people, after the increase in employer National Insurance contributions in October 2024 was defended on the grounds that it fell on employers rather than employees.
Bira said the comments have also prompted a strong reaction from independent retailers on its member forum.
Andrew Goodacre, chief executive, Bira, said: “Once again we have the government trying to tell us that hard-working independent retailers are not considered working people.
“I hoped that a new prime minister and a new chancellor would bury this opinion, as it is quite ridiculous. Retailers have in fact never worked harder for less reward.”
“These are also the same working people who invest in their high street by employing local people and creating a reason to visit and spend money on high streets.
“It is wrong to use semantics to explain a disappointing perspective on how we should interpret the phrase ‘working people’.
“We would like to see a full explanation from the Treasury on this issue, as it is an insult to the many thousands of shop owners across the UK.”
Bira, which works with over 6,000 independent retailers across the UK, said it will continue to press the government for clarity on its position.

items.title: Poundland’s US owner says retailer remains ‘vulnerable’, after talks with ministers
items.summary: Gordon Brothers still in ‘active discussions’ with interested parties and seeking to ‘protect as many jobs as possible’ The US owner of Poundland has said the high street chain remains “challenged and vulnerable” after holding talks with ministers amid government criticism of its handling of the retailer. Gordon Brothers said on Thursday morning that it was still in “active discussions” with interested suitors and had been seeking to “protect as many jobs as possible”. Continue reading...
items.body:
The US owner of Poundland has said the high street chain remains “challenged and vulnerable” after holding talks with ministers amid government criticism of its handling of the retailer.
Gordon Brothers said on Thursday morning that it was still in “active discussions” with interested suitors and had been seeking to “protect as many jobs as possible”.
Poundland filed a notice to appoint administrators last week, with the fate of its 12,000 staff and about 2,000 suppliers uncertain.
Gordon Brothers, the US restructuring specialist that bought Poundland last year for £1 and launched a sale process for the company at the start of September, is under pressure to accept a bid to save the retailer, which is on the brink of collapse despite receiving solvent takeover offers.
Last week the chain filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators, which gave the business 10 working days of breathing space from creditors to secure a potential rescue deal before potentially entering insolvency.
The board of Poundland has lined up the advisory company AlixPartners to run the process after Gordon Brothers ceased providing funding.
On Wednesday, executives from Gordon Brothers and Poundland separately held meetings with government ministers regarding the future of the retailer.
Advisers are still in talks with parties interested in buying the brand and a large number of stores, about two months after a sale process was launched.
However, the chance of Poundland avoiding mass store closures and job losses is shrinking by the day as suppliers have held back on deliveries, hurting its ability to trade.
On Thursday, a spokesperson for Gordon Brothers said: “We are pursuing all avenues through the sale process to find a solution which protects as many jobs as possible and preserves value.
“Work continues at pace, engaging in active discussions on offers with interested parties.
“When Gordon Brothers acquired the business, it was in distress and required a radical restructure, urgent operational change and significant funding, which we provided to support the company’s ability to trade.”
They added: “In spite of our efforts and the tremendous efforts of management to deliver a turnaround, the business remains challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading.
“Our intent throughout the comprehensive sale process has been to protect as many jobs as possible and preserve value in order to deliver the best available outcome for the people, creditors and local communities who care about this business as much as we do.”
There are a number of potential suitors who could buy Poundland – including Northern Ireland’s Martin Property Group, which has offered about £7.5m upfront and the same again in deferred payments over the next two years.
That would pay off about half the £30m shareholder loan, the majority of which was taken on by Gordon Brothers when it bought the company.
Meanwhile, Xyra Group Holdings, a little-known London-based investment company, has offered to pay £12.5m to rescue the business, according to ITV News.
It reported that the firm wants to buy Poundland, retain its existing management team and expand the discount chain overseas. Xyra was approached for comment.
The Irish company Innovest Holdings is also in the mix, and was publicly backed by Reform UK’s Robert Jenrick at the weekend. It is understood it is being advised by the former Reform election candidate Charles Bunker.
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said the owner needed to find a “practical solution” to keep stores open and save jobs.
Asked what his message was to Poundland’s executives, Burnham said: “Focus on the people in your employment … Come up with a practical solution that saves jobs and saves those stores because many of them are viable propositions.
“They’re on high streets. They matter in our communities. There is a solution to be found here. Sit down with us and let’s find it.”
He said the government was “prepared to find what we can do” to help save the chain.
On Thursday, suppliers facing millions of pounds in losses if Poundland collapses told the Guardian that the chain’s US owner should not be permitted to maximise its return at their expense.
It is estimated that Poundland’s collapse could affect up to 30,000 jobs when its supply chain is accounted for.

items.title: Like many others, 87-year-old Janet came to ‘say goodbye’ to the Australian institution that is David Jones
items.summary: As Australia’s oldest department store goes into administration, shoppers mourn its demise amid an uncertain future Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast When Janet Morice thinks of David Jones, she thinks back to postwar Melbourne in 1946, when she would visit the store as a child. “I would put on my best clothes, my mother would put on her hat and gloves, and we would go to afternoon tea at the department store,” she says. Continue reading...
items.body:
When Janet Morice thinks of David Jones, she thinks back to postwar Melbourne in 1946, when she would visit the store as a child.
“I would put on my best clothes, my mother would put on her hat and gloves, and we would go to afternoon tea at the department store,” she says.
Peering through the Christmas displays at the Elizabeth Street store in Sydney’s CBD, the 87-year-old says it is “really, really sad” to think the country’s oldest department store could close.
Metres away, on the ground floor of the flagship store, some shelves sit empty, cleared of their designer accessories within hours of David Jones going into administration on Thursday morning.
“My partner has just said to me ‘Let’s go and say goodbye, because today it’s closing.’ And it’s heartbreaking.”
While David Jones is not shutting immediately, the future of the 188-year-old retailer is highly uncertain, and some underperforming stores are expected to be closed imminently.
The company had fallen behind on rent, culminating in a breakdown of negotiations with its primary landlord, Westfield owner Scentre Group.
The upheaval follows years of steep losses and underperforming stores that left the retailer vulnerable, only for conditions to deteriorate further as high interest rates and cost-of-living pressures led to a pullback in customer spending.
Morice’s partner, Andrew Starr, has shopped at David Jones for more than 40 years. While he says the news is sad, he believes he mourned the department store a long time ago – and feels it “lost its identity” years ago.
“They lost their legacy when they started doing everything up,” he says. “What’s the point of coming into David Jones when you’ve got Chanel and Versace and things like that all the way through it? They had their own brands for a while, and they were good, solid, dependable clothes. Now they’ve sacrificed all that.”
While business appears to be operating as normal on several floors on Thursday afternoon, a few outlets have already stripped their shelves bare.
Employees at a couple of the empty stands tell Guardian Australia they have received orders to shut up shop, with no further details about what will happen to the store or to them.
The upmarket retailer employs more than 6,000 staff across 38 stores.
The David Jones chief executive, Erica Berchtold, has said there is a “well developed plan on how to reset the business” and that the retailer will work with the administrators, receivers and its secured lender.
Grandparents Tim and Louise Cook are among those who stop by the store to “say goodbye” to its famous Christmas display. They have brought their grandson, Billy, fearing it could be his “first and last time”.
The store has been part of the family’s lives for a long time, and they reminisce about many Christmas-time visits. Tim smiles as he recalls how he “got my son’s wedding tie here” four years ago.
“All of our childhood, that was the place we’d go shopping,” Louise says. “It’ll be seriously missed,” Tim adds.
Mark Nelson has spent the morning photographing the Christmas displays after his wife asked him to capture them.
“It could be a very sad occasion, because it could be the last time we see the iconic David Jones Christmas display,” he says. “It is an Australian institution, so it will be a loss.”
The retired university maths professor says he came to love David Jones through his first girlfriend after arriving in Australia from the UK almost 30 years ago.
“She worked at David Jones, so she started getting me to come to David Jones. The girlfriend may have gone, but the attachment to David Jones has continued,” he says. “Don’t tell my wife.”

items.title: Poundland owner in crunch talks as retailer's collapse looms
items.summary: Gordon Brothers will meet Jonathan Reynolds on Wednesday as the investment firm faces scrutiny over Poundland.
items.body:
Poundland owner in crunch talks as retailer's collapse looms
- Published
Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds has met the US-based owners of Poundland as the government hopes to save the retailer from collapse.
The discount chain is on the brink of insolvency and Gordon Brothers, which bought it for Â£1 last June, has rejected a takeover bid which could have saved the 12,000 jobs currently at risk.
A meeting was due to be held on Thursday but was brought forward as the scramble to secure a rescue deal for the firm intensifies.
Gordon Brothers said it is "pursuing all avenues through the sales process" but that Poundland has faced several years of instability and "remains challenged and vulnerable".
The firm said it is "engaging in active discussions on offers with interested parties".
It added: "When Gordon Brothers acquired the business, it was in distress and required a radical restructure, urgent operational change and significant funding, which we provided to support the company's ability to trade."
Both Reynolds and Prime Minister Andy Burnham have questioned why a deal for the future of the business has not been made.
On Wednesday, a source close to business secretary said Reynolds "has been firm that Gordon Brothers must do everything in their power to protect jobs and provide certainty for workers".
"He is pleased to have secured this commitment from Gordon Brothers in the meeting and will continue to hold the company to account and closely monitor developments," the source added.
It is understood that Gordon Brothers made a commitment in the meeting to prioritise bids that will protect workers and units.
However, it is still unclear whether the US investment firm will keep the business together or break it up.
Meanwhile, MPs say they have called in Poundland's owners for questioning on Wednesday 11 November to explain their role in the discount retailer's looming insolvency.
Liam Byrne, chair of Parliament's business committee, said: "Every report suggests Poundland is a viable, profitable business with a future ahead of it and without good reason to let it crash and burn - and then to break it up and sell it off piece by piece.
"We are asking Gordon Brothers to appear before Parliament to explain themselves and tell us just what it is that's preventing them from accepting the fully-funded deal on the table to save more than 12,000 jobs."
Business Minister Kate Dearden and union representatives met Poundland's managing director Barry Williams on Wednesday.
Mr Williams told the BBC that Poundland is profitable and sales were growing.
"We're back in profit and it has a bright future ahead of it if it's allowed to deliver that," he said.
Poundland has filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators, which protects it from its creditors until next Thursday.
Asked what his message for Poundland's owner was, Burnham said Gordon Brothers should "focus on the people in your employment" and "come up with a practical solution that saves jobs and saves those stores".
"There is a solution to be found here, sit down with us and let's find it," he added.
The meeting comes after a major Poundland supplier has said it will lose millions of pounds if the retailer goes bust.
Adam Turner, sales director at Bradford-based Highcrest Retail Brands, said Poundland was one of its biggest customers and its collapse would cost it "a few million" in lost sales.
The family owned business mainly sells confectionery to Poundland and turns over about Â£50m.
Turner said the firm becoming insolvent would leave a substantial gap in its balance sheet next year.
Highcrest was a "longstanding business that can stomach this", Turner said. But he warned other medium and small suppliers to the retailer have told him that "if Poundland goes under, so do they".
This echoes a warning from Poundland founder Steve Smith on Monday that two or three thousand suppliers to the firm, which only work for Poundland, would be directly affected by its collapse.
Not only would Poundland's 12,000 staff be affected in that case, but potentially up to 30,000 overall, he told the BBC on Wednesday.
He said he was "amazed" Poundland was being put into administration, pointing to the profitability of the company.
"Also, there's two offers on the table from some really good people," he added.
"All I'm asking is for Gordon Brothers to see if they can put a deal together."
Gordon Brothers said Walsall-based Poundland is "still not cash generative at a sustainable level" because of the economic issues it faces.
If Poundland's stores are sold to new buyers, some of the employees may get new jobs on the same premises.
However, it is understood that buyers are only interested in about half the stores at present â meaning roughly 6,000 employees would not be re-employed.
- Poundland's founder offers to invest in firm 
  - Published4 days ago
High stock levels
If Poundland goes under, suppliers will be getting "pennies in the pound" back from the administration, he said, which is "very upsetting" â although he still hopes a deal can be done so Poundland can remain solvent.
Poundland owners Gordon Brothers will be a secured creditor, which means they are first in line to get their money back, and suppliers "who have done nothing wrong" will take the financial hit.
"It's sad. It's a nightmare for us all to be honest with you. It's not just the suppliers, it's the staff at Poundland, some of these guys have been there for many years.
"It's from the warehouse staff all the way to the shop staff to everybody within head office. It's a massive ripple effect through the supply chain," he added.
Turner said he had no knowledge of whether Gordon Brothers had deliberately timed the process of Poundland going into administration so it could take advantage of having high stock levels, which it can then sell.
One of the ways Gordon Brothers makes money is through stock liquidations â selling off stock from collapsed businesses.
One insider familiar with the situation told the BBC that the timing of Poundland facing collapse was "odd" â most retailers don't fall over in the run-up to Christmas.
Ministers' questions
Dearden has said the government doesn't want to interfere with "current ongoing commercial negotiations", but that ministers want "clarity" on the plans for the retailer.
"It's absolutely legitimate for this government to ask the business if they're doing everything they can to protect employees and suppliers up and down the country," she added.
Dearden told MPs that the government would be ready to help the company's employees if Poundland collapses.
The head of Gordon Brothers' European operations reportedly told the government that the firm stood by its stewardship and had given Poundland Â£85m in additional financing since its purchase in 2025.
Get in touch
Are you affected by issues discussed in this story? Do you work for Poundland? Share your experiences.

items.title: Wayvia and Euronics team to connect brands, retailers and shoppers across 36 global markets
items.summary: Wayvia has announced a partnership with Euronics International focused on building a more connected digital shopping ecosystem for brands, Euronics’ retailers and the consumers they serve.The partnership, powered by Wayvia’s Where to Buy technology, will enable brands to directly connect shoppers wh
items.body:
Wayvia has announced a partnership with Euronics International focused on building a more connected digital shopping ecosystem for brands, Euronics’ retailers and the consumers they serve.
The partnership, powered by Wayvia’s Where to Buy technology, will enable brands to directly connect shoppers who discover products on their websites to more than 6,500 stores and online retailers across the Euronics network, which spans 36 markets in Europe and Asia.
“Euronics is one of the most trusted names in consumer electronics retail, and millions of customers rely on its members for the technology that's now central to all our lives,” says Anthony Ferry, Co-founder and CEO at Wayvia. “Through this partnership, we are helping to build the digital ecosystem that brands and Euronics retailers need to grow in an increasingly complex environment where consumer journeys are becoming ever more personalised.”
“The consumer electronics market is more competitive than ever, and today’s consumers expect and deserve a seamless journey from product discovery to purchase,” says John Olsen, CEO at Euronics International.
“Our partnership with Wayvia creates a stronger connection between brands, our members and consumers. Our retailers are a key part of brands’ go-to-market strategies, combining omnichannel capabilities with trusted advice, local expertise and a compelling in-store experience."
"By connecting brand websites with this retail network, we can make the consumer journey more seamless while supporting both our members and our suppliers. We have always believed that suppliers, retailers and technology partners achieve the most when they work together.”
Wayvia’s technology integrates Euronics’ product feeds and, where available, local store availability data, enabling shoppers to identify retailers that stock the products they discover on brand websites and choose where to purchase. Wayvia also provides visibility into referral traffic and conversions, helping Euronics and its members better understand how digital product discovery translates into sales.
The pair plan to deepen their partnership by expanding sales data sharing across Euronics members and extending local in-store availability to more markets.

items.title: JD Sports rolls out Zebra Technologies RFID tech across 414 stores in UK and Ireland
items.summary: Zebra Technologies says that it has helped JD Sports to achieve 98% on-shelf availability and 20% faster replenishment, so high demand sizes move from the storeroom to the shelf when and where customers want them.JD Sports has nearly 5,000 stores across 46 countries. As the retailer scaled, inventor
items.body:
Zebra Technologies says that it has helped JD Sports to achieve 98% on-shelf availability and 20% faster replenishment, so high demand sizes move from the storeroom to the shelf when and where customers want them.
JD Sports has nearly 5,000 stores across 46 countries. As the retailer scaled, inventory visibility in stores remained a challenge. To reliably offer one-hour Click & Collect or 30-minute delivery, the stock count needed to be accurate. It sought a real-time inventory visibility solution that could support omnichannel retail, was easy for retail assistants to use and fast to roll-out across stores.
A pilot across five stores highlighted the capabilities of Zebra’s TC2 Series mobile computers paired with RFD40 UHF RFID sleds to read tags faster and at greater range. JD Sports also selected Zebra OneCare which allows its store associates to address everyday wear and tear and accidental damage by simply swapping devices at no cost if something breaks.
Alongside Zebra, JD Sports worked with Renovotec, a Zebra partner who led the device deployment, and Checkpoint Systems, a Zebra eegistered ISV who integrated its ItemOptix software, giving a single view of inventory data across the retailer.
"What Zebra gives us is the ability to scale with trust,” says Daniel McGrath, Head of Customer Operations, JD Sports. “Things just land and work. Colleagues open a box, turn it on, and they are up and running. That lets our teams spend their time where it matters: with the customer.”
The first store went live in 76 days, with roll-out at 26 additional stores a week on average, reaching 414 locations across the UK and Ireland in roughly three months.
An associate clips a RFID sled onto the mobile computer they already use for daily tasks and walks the floor and stockroom, sweeping rails and shelves as the reader logs every tagged item in range and builds a live count on screen. In some cases, a whole store can be covered in a single pass.
Store associates now move 95% more inventory from the storeroom to shop floor and spend less time on stock counting. Stores can run this process from twice a week, or even daily, allowing them to keep shelves and the inventory management system in sync.
The same visibility is also helping JD Sports proactively tackle loss, as teams can identify and investigate issues much sooner. They can see where loss is happening rather than waiting for a 90- or 180-day audit.
“Retailers like JD Sports demonstrate the effectiveness of Zebra’s Modern Store framework, and the outcomes we and our partners deliver for both retailers and their shoppers,” says Mark Thomson, Retail Strategy Director EMEA, Zebra Technologies. “Together, we’re making work better every day for retailers and their frontline workers.”

items.title: Brits set for record £28.52 billion festive online spend amid surge in AI driven shopping
items.summary: British consumers will splash out a record £28.52 billion online between 1st November and 31st December 2026, according to research released by Adobe.Spending this year is anticipated to increase by 6.2% year-on-year (YoY) as total Q4 (October–December) e-commerce spend is projected to reach £4
items.body:
British consumers will splash out a record £28.52 billion online between 1st November and 31st December 2026, according to research released by Adobe.
Spending this year is anticipated to increase by 6.2% year-on-year (YoY) as total Q4 (October–December) e-commerce spend is projected to reach £40 billion (+6.4% YoY). Powered by Adobe Analytics, the research analyses direct consumer transactions across hundreds of billions of visits to UK retailer websites, tracking 100 million SKUs across 18 product categories.
The findings reveal a consumer base that is spending with greater intent, leveraging deep online price advantages, relying on social and influencer discovery, and increasingly turning to generative AI assistants to uncover the best value.
The four-day Cyber Weekend (27th November – 30th November) is expected to be the most lucrative shopping period of the year, generating £4.05 billion in online spend and averaging more than £1 billion in online sales per day (+6.6% YoY).
Black Friday (27th November) remains the single biggest online spending day of the year at £1.24 billion, growing 7.1% YoY. Cyber Monday (30th November) will experience the fastest growth rate of the weekend at 7.6% YoY, surpassing £1 billion in daily online spend for the first time.
Discounts are projected to climb steadily throughout November - from 12% in early November to 18% just before Black Friday - before peaking at 25% off from the start of Cyber Weekend.
Consumers are leveraging the peak discount window to purchase higher-value items that were previously outside of their budgets with online prices expected to be down by an average of 2.5% YoY. Overall, the number of units sold from the most expensive quartile of products is expected to rise by more than 13%, particularly in the personal care (+38%), sporting goods (+34%), and electronics (+30%) categories.
Simultaneously, consumers are actively using seasonal promotions to stock up on everyday household essentials. During Cyber Week, online orders for everyday items are projected to surge compared to pre-season baselines, led by clothing basics (+215%), personal care and beauty (+148%), baby products (+84%), and household cleaning (+47%).
Vivek Pandya, Director of Adobe Digital Insights, comments: "UK shoppers are set to spend a record £28.52 billion online this holiday season, taking advantage of lower online prices and peak discounting moments to buy both higher-priced items and household essentials ahead of the festive period."
"This year also sees a shift in how consumers are discovering, evaluating and purchasing products, as they increasingly turn to generative AI, social media and influencers to guide their buying decisions and direct them to retail sites.”
British shoppers are increasingly bypassing traditional search engines, turning instead to generative AI tools, social media platforms, and creator content as trusted advisors for gift discovery and purchasing journeys. Notably, retail traffic driven by generative AI platforms is projected to surge by 214% YoY in November and December, accelerating rapidly from a 111% YoY increase in September. Equally, revenue share from social networks (+24% YoY) and influencer partnerships (+7% YoY) are forecast to lead marketing channel growth.
Rather than subsiding after Christmas, AI usage is expected to sustain momentum well into post-holiday sales. Categories experiencing the strongest AI referral boosts include video games, toys, electronics, appliances, jewellery, and personal care.
"For retailers, winning this festive season requires more than just slashing prices. Brands must ensure that value is transparent, and that product data, educational buying guides, and customer support are clear and easily surfaced across the AI and social ecosystems guiding consumer decisions," Pandya concludes.

items.body:
ESW has announced a partnership with Tecnica Group to support the global e-commerce expansion of Moon Boot, its winter footwear and lifestyle brand.
ESW is providing Moon Boot with an end-to-end e-commerce solution spanning fulfilment, shipping and returns, merchant of record (MOR) services, localisation and B2B2C.
The partnership forms part of a wider transformation of Moon Boot’s e-commerce operations, including its migration from Salesforce Commerce to Shopify. Arsenalia is acting as systems integrator and leading the Shopify replatforming, working alongside Tecnica Group and ESW to integrate the new platform.
The model supports Moon Boot in key markets including the United States, combining international fulfilment and logistics with the cross-border infrastructure needed to serve customers in-market.
Andrea Antonioli, eCommerce Strategy & Operations Manager at Moon Boot says: “As we expand our international ecommerce operations, we need a model that can support the complexity of serving customers across different markets. ESW brings together the fulfilment, logistics and cross-border capabilities we need within one solution, while giving us the flexibility we need as the business grows. We are excited to get the partnership underway.”
Federica Ronchi, VP Sales, Southern Europe at ESW, says: “Moon Boot already has a highly international customer base and clear demand across key global markets."
"As Tecnica Group evolves its e-commerce operations, we’re bringing fulfilment, logistics and cross-border commerce together to help Moon Boot manage that international demand without adding complexity for its internal teams. It’s about making it easier to serve customers across markets and giving the business room to grow its direct-to-consumer operations over time.”
Moon Boot is now live with ESW across the United States, France, Germany, Italy, the United Kingdom, Canada and Spain, with plans to extend the partnership to other Tecnica Group brands in the future.

items.title: David Jones goes into administration, with store closures expected and thousands of jobs at risk
items.summary: Future of Australia’s upmarket department store in jeopardy after years of steep losses, and outer suburban and regional locations vulnerable Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Australia’s premier upmarket department store David Jones has collapsed into voluntary administration, putting thousands of jobs at risk amid warnings “difficult decisions” lie ahead to salvage the 188-year-old retailer. The upheaval follows years of steep losses and underperforming stores that left the heritage retailer falling behind on rent, culminating in a breakdown of negotiations with its primary landlord, Westfield owner Scentre Group. Continue reading...
items.body:
Australia’s premier upmarket department store David Jones has collapsed into voluntary administration, putting thousands of jobs at risk amid warnings “difficult decisions” lie ahead to salvage the 188-year-old retailer.
The upheaval follows years of steep losses and underperforming stores that left the heritage retailer falling behind on rent, culminating in a breakdown of negotiations with its primary landlord, Westfield owner Scentre Group.
Staff were informed on Thursday that the David Jones board had appointed administrators from McGrathNicol, before the retailer’s main financier promptly installed FTI Consulting as receivers.
Under the dual appointment, FTI will take day-to-day control of operations, while administrators McGrathNicol seek a buyer or fresh injection of capital.
Christopher Hill, of FTI Consulting, said the process allowed for “an opportunity to restructure the business”.
“We will manage this process carefully, mindful of the impact on some stakeholders but also recognising the need for difficult decisions,” Hill said.
The process will almost certainly trigger immediate store closures, though receivers will try keep the core network open.
Analysts expect closures to hit outer suburban and regional mall locations hardest, likely sparing premier CBD flagship stores.
David Jones employs more than 6,000 staff across a network of 38 stores.
The David Jones chief executive, Erica Berchtold, said there was a “well developed plan on how to reset the business” and that the retailer would work with the administrators, receivers and its secured lender.
Creditors are scheduled to meet next week, according to the Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees’ Association.
The national secretary of the SDA, Gerard Dwyer, told the ABC the top priority was to retain as many jobs as possible.
“We do not want to see the end of David Jones, so perhaps it is a smaller model that then rebuilds and goes from there,” Dwyer said.
“Smaller is better than no David Jones, and a smaller David Jones can then deal with some of the challenges that they’ve obviously been facing.”
The administration could leave unsecured creditors with substantial losses, with unpaid product suppliers, some of which had already begun redirecting stock to their own retail outlets, and shoppers holding unredeemed gift vouchers most at risk.
Gift cards may be ‘worthless’ soon
Angus Kidman, from consumer comparison site Finder, said customers with David Jones gift cards should use them as soon as possible.
“If the business doesn’t find a buyer, that gift card will almost certainly be worthless,” Kidman said.
“Stores appear to be accepting gift cards for now, so don’t delay. That also applies to any discounts you’ve earned through David Jones Rewards.”
The collapse marks the first time David Jones has been in administration, having previously weathered nearly two centuries while cycling through almost every type of ownership model, from public listing to foreign conglomerate ownership and, most recently, private equity.
Anchorage Capital Partners, which bought David Jones from South Africa’s Woolworths in 2023, has now lost operational control after failing to turn the struggling retailer around.
It could re-bid for the business through the administration process or a rival buyer, such as billionaire businessman Solomon Lew, who controls Myer, may get involved.
The retailer’s main landlord, Scentre, said on Wednesday that David Jones had not paid rent since September.
“We have made a generous offer to Anchorage Capital that would have facilitated the continuation of David Jones trading and that offer has disappointingly been rejected by them,” Scentre said in a statement.

items.title: OECD: AI compute now a strategic asset as UK bets £2bn
items.summary: <p>Artificial intelligence (AI) compute has become a strategic national asset, with venture capital for AI infrastructure more than doubling year-on-year to $123.9bn in 2025. Meanwhile, the UK’s commitment to spend up to £2bn on its Compute Roadmap is one of the leading bets placed by governments around the world.</p> <p>That’s according to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), which published its <em>Digital economy and society outlook 2026</em> today.</p> <p>In the report, the OECD says AI compute now sits alongside data, algorithms and skills as a determinant of who can build and deploy advanced AI systems. It says venture capital investment in AI firms in IT infrastructure and hosting rose from $54.5bn in 2024 to $123.9bn in 2025, which is the largest increase since 2012.</p> <p>The report namechecks the <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/uk-compute-roadmap/uk-compute-roadmap">
items.body:
Victoria - Fotolia
OECD: AI compute now a strategic asset as UK bets £2bn
Venture capital for artificial intelligence firms in IT infrastructure and hosting rose from $54.5bn to $123.9bn, while the OECD says compute now shapes which countries can build advanced AI
Artificial intelligence (AI) compute has become a strategic national asset, with venture capital for AI infrastructure more than doubling year-on-year to $123.9bn in 2025. Meanwhile, the UK’s commitment to spend up to £2bn on its Compute Roadmap is one of the leading bets placed by governments around the world.
That’s according to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), which published its Digital economy and society outlook 2026 today.
In the report, the OECD says AI compute now sits alongside data, algorithms and skills as a determinant of who can build and deploy advanced AI systems. It says venture capital investment in AI firms in IT infrastructure and hosting rose from $54.5bn in 2024 to $123.9bn in 2025, which is the largest increase since 2012.
The report namechecks the UK Compute Roadmap, launched in 2025 with up to £2bn pledged to “deliver a holistic and user-centred compute ecosystem” and £1bn to expand the AI Research Resource, plus a new national supercomputing service. It also notes the emergence of neocloud providers of infrastructure purpose-built for AI workloads, such as the UK’s Nscale, the US’s CoreWeave and Netherlands-headquartered Nebius.
The OECD is an intergovernmental body whose member governments use it to agree non-binding standards for digital policy. Its reports do not set law, but governments fold their recommendations into regulation – such as the EU AI Act – so the organisation is an early indicator of auditability and data governance requirements that can later become compliance obligations.
The OECD warns in the report that sizeable capital investment in infrastructure, networking and energy access gives traditional hyperscalers a considerable market advantage, which is compounded by developer ecosystems and hardware partnerships that build dependencies. Newer AI-specific providers may expand, it says, but buyers will likely continue to rely on existing hyperscaler capacity – a familiar dynamic for UK organisations balancing cloud lock-in against AI ambition.
The report flags two bottlenecks that may limit compute performance. The first is that accelerator performance has tripled every two years while memory (DRAM) has scaled at just 1.6 times over the same period – a gap it calls “the memory wall”, which can leave processors idle and waiting for data. Moving data between chips forms a second constraint – “the interconnect wall”, which slows distributed training and inference across racks and nodes.
For IT leaders, it says, compute also collides with energy and planning. The OECD notes that hyperscale datacentre buildouts can take up to three years, while securing multi-gigawatt power can take more than four – a mismatch that already shapes grid connection queues and the UK’s push towards 6GW of AI-capable capacity.
“Alongside data, algorithms and skills, AI compute has emerged as a strategic asset with profound implications for innovation and competitiveness,” the report says.
Other government investments in AI include Canada, which committed C$2bn (approx. £1bn) to a Sovereign AI Compute Strategy in 2024; the EU, which will channel €7bn (approx. £5.5bn) through its EuroHPC joint undertaking for 2021-27; and the US, which backs the Stargate datacentre venture.
The OECD report finds that 60% of member countries now assign national digital strategy to a dedicated digital ministry, up from 24% in 2016, and that cyber security has risen to the second-highest policy priority.
The scale of the figures demands caution, the report says. “Figures often reflect announcements and commitments rather than implementation,” it says, with delivery dependent on supply chain resilience, energy and water availability, and shifting national priorities.
On that reading, the investment surge can be viewed as a statement of intent rather than evidence of built capacity. Turning the UK’s £2bn into operational infrastructure will depend on grid and planning constraints that decide whether promised datacentres arrive on time.
Read more about AI compute and datacentres
- Hit the north! UK datacentre focus shifts to M62 and points north: Barbour ABI data shows an 8GW datacentre pipeline concentrated in the north and Scotland, with London and the M4 corridor about 25% of projected capacity.
- Enormous AI growth zone datacentre gets planning approval: A planned 1GW AI growth zone facility – equal to more than 2% of current UK electricity demand – gains consent.

items.title: Australia's oldest department store David Jones folds after 188 years
items.summary: The brand's 38 physical stores and online site will continue to operate while receivers review its operations.
items.body:
Australia's oldest department store David Jones folds after 188 years
- Published
David Jones, Australia's oldest department store chain, has gone into voluntary administration, putting thousands of jobs at risk.
It comes after years of financial struggles for the 188-year-old retailer - known locally as DJs - as customers desert traditional shops for online shopping.
David Jones's physical and online stores will continue to operate while receivers FTI Consulting review the company, said voluntary administrators McGrathNicol.
"David Jones is an iconic company and so many Australians have stories and memories of visiting DJ's stores," said its CEO Erica Berthold, adding the brand has a "well-developed plan" to "reset the business for the future".
Berthold thanked "customers, our team members and our partners for their continued support of David Jones through this period".
David Jones employs about 6,000 staff and has 38 physical stores, with 17 of those in Westfield shopping centres.
Hours before the board voted to go into administration, Scentre - which owns Westfield - said the retailer had not paid its rent for October and was "therefore in breach" of its tenancy agreement.
"We understand the current retail trading environment, rising costs, a significant and outdated retail footprint, and supply chain challenges have led to this point," said Christopher Hill from receivers FTI Consulting.
By appointing administrators and receivers, David Jones will get "breathing space" and a chance to restructure the business, Hill said.
For many Australians, David Jones - and its trademark black-and-white houndstooth design - represented luxury.
But its collapse signalled the "death knell" for the department store format, said Jana Bowden, who teaches marketing at Macquarie University's Business School.
"It was once the epitome of glamour shopping in Australia - the Aussie version of Harrods," she said, "a place you would go to see and be a part of the glitz and glamour, where you could marvel at all the premium luxury labels, and feel like you'd made it."
Visiting the flagship city stores in Sydney and Melbourne was also a ritual for many Australian families, especially to see the festive Christmas window displays.
"People would travel from hours away from the city just to see those windows and experience the magic," Bowden said, but in recent years, the brand had lost its shine.
"The city stores have retained their upper end airs and graces, but the suburban stores leave a lot to be desired â they're mundane, they lack excitement and there's definitely no glitz," she said.
During Queen Elizabeth II's first visit to Sydney in 1954, the then-27-year-old monarch attended a banquet dinner on the seventh floor of the Elizabeth St store, according to the Sydney Morning Herald.

items.title: Once it was a £1 hanger. Now it’s a £15 locker. Why do cloakrooms cost so much on a night out?
items.summary: The cost of checking your coat or bag is galloping ahead of other – also rising – prices at venues. We explain the surprisingly complex reasons why Not long ago, it cost just £2 to put a coat or a heavily stuffed tote bag in a cloakroom on a night out. But over the course of the 2020s, that cost has increased to more than £13 in some UK venues. At the Outernet Live venue complex in London’s Soho, it costs £11 to put a bag in a large locker. It’s £9 at east London nightclub Fold, and at north London’s Drumsheds, the UK’s biggest nightclub, they cost up to £13.20 . At the Warehouse Project in Manchester, large bags must be stored at a nearby Premier Inn at £11.99 per locker. Manchester’s Co-op Live Arena has a dedicated bag storage facility which costs £15 for large bags. It’s £9.99 near the 3,000-capacity Edinburgh Playhouse and £9.90 at Testbed in Leeds. How have double-digit cloakroom costs like these been normalised? Continue reading...
items.body:
Not long ago, it cost just £2 to put a coat or a heavily stuffed tote bag in a cloakroom on a night out. But over the course of the 2020s, that cost has increased to more than £13 in some UK venues.
At the Outernet Live venue complex in London’s Soho, it costs £11 to put a bag in a large locker. It’s £9 at east London nightclub Fold, and at north London’s Drumsheds, the UK’s biggest nightclub, they cost up to £13.20 . At the Warehouse Project in Manchester, large bags must be stored at a nearby Premier Inn at £11.99 per locker. Manchester’s Co-op Live Arena has a dedicated bag storage facility which costs £15 for large bags. It’s £9.99 near the 3,000-capacity Edinburgh Playhouse and £9.90 at Testbed in Leeds. How have double-digit cloakroom costs like these been normalised?
The price rises are helping to push average spending per head on a night out from £20.95 in 2020 to £28.06 in 2026, according to Night Time Industries Association. “For years, nightlife businesses have faced relentless increases in the cost of operating, from energy and employment to taxation, business rates and supply chains,” says chief executive Michael Kill. “Many have had no choice but to pass some of those costs on to consumers simply to keep their doors open. But the reality is that consumers have now hit an affordability ceiling.”
With consumers spending less on alcohol, locker systems and cloakrooms offer premises a way to make some of that money back, but, Kill says, “the consumer cannot be the industry’s financial shock absorber indefinitely”.
UK storage policy changed after the 2017 attack at an Ariana Grande concert in Manchester Arena which killed 22 people and injured more than 1,000. “Martyn’s law” legislation requires “appropriate public protection measures” at public events to reduce the risk and impact of terror attacks. It led to many venues – including the nationwide network of 18 Academy Music Group sites – banning bags over A4 size entirely and offloading them to external lockers or storage partners. In London, these are often kebab shops, restaurants and barbers.
Carrie Wang, a London-based spin instructor, was buzzing to see Hot Chip at O2 Academy Brixton until she learned her near-empty tote bag had to be stored in a kebab shop round the corner. “I was fuming,” Wang says. “They charged me £10 and it wasn’t a proper facility, it was just a random storage room – it’s not like they had lockers and my things were actually safe there.” Academy Music Group did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
Ahmed Khan is the owner of Kentish Delight, a kebab shop in Kentish Town. He says that in 2022, O2 Kentish Town Forum’s management asked if he had any spare space in the takeaway. “They had a look and said my premises are perfect and secure for the customer – and I said yes, why not?” Khan charges £5 per bag and says nothing has ever gone missing. “Although the bag people never buy kebabs.”
The high costs and added logistics mean that some people are taking risks with their belongings. At an AEW wrestling event at Wembley Arena, fans were directed to a nearby Premier Inn to stow their bags, at £10 a pop with long queues.
Soul singer Danny Toeman decided to stuff his rucksack behind a carpark vending machine. “I could stuff most of the valuable contents into my pockets,” says Toeman. “So I thought: let’s just stash it somewhere and if it gets stolen, so what?”
That in itself is a security risk – if staff had seen Toeman’s backpack, the venue could have been evacuated. But it’s become commonplace. One Reddit user opted to hide their bag outside the O2 Academy in Southampton. “They will literally not let you in,” they wrote. “I was forced to leave it outside the building entirely and it was stolen when I came out.”
Willem Pelle is head of sales at eLockers, a Dutch company working with many UK nightclubs including Drumsheds, Fold and Warehouse Project. “When we expanded into the UK, we saw that many venues were facing staffing challenges following Covid, making traditional cloakrooms increasingly difficult to operate,” Pelle says.
London is their main UK market, with Manchester a close second. Pelle says there is typically no upfront cost for the venue, which gets to share the takings with eLockers, adding: “It’s important that the pricing works for both the venue and its customers, while creating a sustainable additional revenue stream.”
Some clubbers have reported benefits to lockers, such as those at Drumsheds, where you can put stuff in and out – allowing for outfit changes during an event. But not all venues opt to install expensive locker systems. At Hackney Bath House, the cloakroom is free. Sneaky Pete’s in Edinburgh installed lockers in 2012 and still charge £2 per locker. Peckham’s 200-capacity club the Carpet Shop charges £3 per item: “No need to charge more, it’s a tiny bit of space and a rail,” says general manager Cam Prentis.
He sees the cloakroom as a valuable part of the club experience in its own right. Upstairs and away from the bustle, it’s where staff and punters can have a break and a chat. “Whoever’s on the cloakroom has their own music playing,” Cam says. Unlike at an unstaffed array of lockers or the back room of a kebab shop, “it’s a vibe up there”.
Some names have been changed

items.title: Poundland could be nationalised to save it from collapse, says Labour business minister
items.summary: Poundland could be nationalised to save it from collapse, a government minister suggested today.
items.body:
Poundland could be nationalised to save it from collapse, says Labour business minister
Poundland could be nationalised to save it from collapse, a government minister suggested today.
Business minister Lord Leong refused to rule out a taxpayer subsidy or even full-blown state control of the troubled discount chain.
The comment was seized on by the Tories as evidence of Labour chaos and a lack of understanding of business.
It came as Andy Burnham said the government was ‘prepared to find what we can do’ to help save the chain.
Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said nationalising Poundland would be ‘insane’.
He added: 'The hard truth is that in a dynamic economy, businesses are created, whilst others sadly fail. We cannot expect taxpayers to step in and solve all of life's problems.
‘Labour business policy is in chaos. When you get a government with so little business experience as this one, this is what results.’
Poundland is on the brink of collapse - putting 600 stores and 12,000 jobs at risk
Poundland, which was bought by private equity group Gordon Brothers for £1 last year, could crash into administration as early as this week – putting 600 stores and 12,000 jobs at risk in the run-up to Christmas.
A Poundland distribution centre employing 270 staff in Makerfield – Mr Burnham’s constituency in Greater Manchester – is also at risk.
Asked what his message was to Poundland owners and executives, the Prime Minister said: ‘Focus on the people in your employment.
‘Come up with a practical solution that saves jobs and saves those stores because many of them are viable propositions.
‘They’re on high streets. They matter in our communities. There is a solution to be found here. Sit down with us and let’s find it.’
Speaking to reporters while attending the Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting in Antigua, Mr Burnham acknowledged there was a limit to what ministers could do but he suggested there were ways forward for the firm.
‘There’s always a limit, but we’re prepared to to find what we can do,’ he said.
‘We believe in this instance there is a solution. There are many viable outlets here. Other retailers are expressing interest. Get around the table. Let’s find a solution.’
The comments came as Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds was set to meet US-based Gordon Brothers amid Government criticism of their handling of the retailer.
Business minister Kate Dearden is also due to hold talks with Poundland’s chief executive and chief finance officer.
Asked in the House of Lords if he could ‘rule out specific Poundland subsidy or nationalisation as a solution’, Lord Leong said: ‘The answer is no.’
He was later slapped down by departmental officials who said he had ‘misspoken’.
A Whitehall source added: 'There are no plans to nationalise Poundland.'
Company advisers are still in talks with parties interested in buying the brand and swathes of stores, around two months after a sale process was launched.
Tesco has held talks over proposals to buy up to 150 Poundland stores while Poundstretcher owner Fortress also showed its interest in purchasing as many as 250 shops.
It is understood that other grocery chains, such as Iceland and Lidl, are also in the frame to acquire some stores.
Wilko and The Range owner CDS Superstores and B&M have also expressed their interest in sites.
Downing Street has been critical of Gordon Brothers’ handling of the sale process.
‘It appears they’re not acting in the best interests of their loyal UK staff and stores,’ the Prime Minister’s official spokesman said.
It is an ‘extremely worrying situation for Poundland staff, their families and communities’ and the Government was staying close to the situation, the spokesman said.
‘Both the Prime Minister and the Business Secretary have been clear: they want to know what’s happening and Gordon Brothers need to explain why they haven’t accepted any offer to keep the company going.’
Gordon Brothers could also face questioning in Parliament over its actions.
Liam Byrne said the Commons Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee which he chairs has ‘issued a request to Gordon Brothers to come before us next week to answer questions’.
The crisis at Poundland has raised fresh questions over private equity ownership of household names across Britian’s high streets and beyond.
Other big firms taken over by private equity include struggling supermarket chains Asda and Morrisons.
Richard Walker, the boss of Iceland, accused Gordon Brothers of ‘private equity opportunism’ amid fears it would rather put Poundland into administration and sell off sites piecemeal than find a buyer to rescue the whole business.
He said: ‘You could say that it’s in my own interest to have one less competitor on the high street. But I say that we need our high streets to be places offering variety and vitality – with as many shops as we can sustain trading successfully, satisfying customers and providing good jobs.
‘Sure, it’s a tough market. As I’ve long argued, retail just gets harder and harder – not helped by government imposing more and more cost and complexity on businesses.
‘But Poundland isn’t bust. All the signs are that it’s been trading OK. Administration seems more about private equity opportunism than business necessity.
‘Good capitalism is about doing the right thing by our colleagues, customers and communities. Do that, and the profits follow.’
Bally Auluk, Usdaw national officer, said: 'This afternoon I am meeting with Employment Minister Kate Dearden, along with Poundland’s senior management team.
'We welcome the Government’s commitment to support our members and help to save jobs, including the Prime Minister’s statement today.
'We are aware that Poundland’s owners are set to meet with the Business Secretary, which is welcome, but we urge Gordon Brothers to engage directly with Usdaw as the trade union for Poundland staff, which they have so far refused to do.'
